title: What plants need, and how to test it fairly

summary.text: Moong grown in a dark cupboard grows taller than moong on a windowsill. But the plants are pale and thin, and they fall over. So what does a plant really need? They need light, water, air, warmth and minerals from the soil, each in the right amount. Your child finds this out with fair tests, which change only one thing at a time. They grow moong in the light and in the dark, and measure them with a ruler every few days. They can also test too little and too much water, and cold against warmth.
summary.art: Three rows of paper cups of moong seedlings on a windowsill: one row green and sturdy in the sun, one row tall and yellow under a lifted cardboard box, one row drooping beside a dish of water, with a child measuring one seedling with a school ruler.

intro.hook: Have you seen moong sprouts grown in a closed box, or a potato that has sat in a dark kitchen basket? Their shoots are white or pale yellow, not green. Why?
intro.text: Sprouts grown in a closed tiffin, and potato shoots in a dark basket, come out long and pale. They are alive, and they grow fast. The only thing they were missing was light. So what does a plant really need? Is it light, water, warmth or soil? And how could you find out for sure, without guessing? In this unit you find out with fair tests, changing one thing at a time.
intro.art: A kitchen basket tipped open to show a potato with long, pale, thin shoots, beside an open steel tiffin of moong sprouts with white shoots.

outcomes: I can say what a plant needs to grow well: light, water, air, warmth and minerals, each in the right amount.
I can plan and run a fair test of light, water or warmth. I change only one thing and keep everything else the same.
I can measure a plant's height in centimetres and millimetres, at the same time each day. I can write it in a results table.
I can show my results in a bar chart and write a conclusion: what I think, what I saw, and why.
I can read a plant's clues, like tall and pale, wilting, or yellow with soggy soil, and say which need is missing.
I can explain that more is not always better. Too much water, too much heat or too much cold harms a plant, and each kind of plant has their own 'just right'.
I can give big examples. Plants sense light and warmth with special molecules. People grow plants in space. Scientists still have open questions about how plants sense warmth.

terms.meaning: Something a living thing must have to stay alive and healthy.
terms.example: You need food, water and air. A plant needs light, water, air, warmth and minerals.
terms.art: A child and a tulsi plant side by side, each with small pictures of what they need floating above them.

terms.meaning: A very young plant that has just grown out of their seed.
terms.example: A moong seedling has a thin stem and two small round leaves.
terms.art: A moong seedling in a paper cup with two round leaves.

terms.meaning: Getting bigger. A plant grows taller, grows more leaves and grows longer roots.
terms.example: A moong seedling can grow from 1 centimetre to 10 centimetres tall in a week.
terms.art: The same seedling drawn on three days, a little taller each time.

terms.meaning: What lets us see. For a plant, light is also the energy they use to make their own food.
terms.example: Sunlight through a window. A plant on a windowsill leans towards it.
terms.art: A plant on a windowsill leaning towards a sunny window.

terms.meaning: How hot or cold something is. We measure it in degrees Celsius, written °C.
terms.example: A cool room in winter might be 18 °C. A hot afternoon in May might be 40 °C.
terms.art: A thermometer beside a cup of ice and a thermometer beside a sunny window.

terms.meaning: A tool that measures temperature. A coloured liquid or a number shows how hot it is.
terms.example: A room thermometer on the wall shows 28 °C.
terms.art: A simple room thermometer with a red line at 28 degrees.

terms.meaning: Substances in soil that a plant needs in tiny amounts, such as nitrogen and iron. They dissolve in water, and the roots take them in with the water.
terms.example: Compost and cow dung add minerals to soil.
terms.art: A handful of dark compost with a few tiny glowing specks.

terms.meaning: A test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same. Then you know what caused the result.
terms.example: To test light, put two cups of the same seedlings in the light and the dark, and give both the same water.
terms.art: Two identical cups of seedlings, one under a box, with the same watering spoon beside each.

terms.meaning: In a fair test, the one thing you choose to change on purpose. Scientists call it the variable.
terms.example: In the light test, the thing we change is light: one cup gets light, one does not.
terms.art: A big arrow pointing at a cardboard box over one cup.

terms.meaning: In a fair test, what you look at or measure to see what happened.
terms.example: The height of the seedlings, in centimetres.
terms.art: A ruler standing beside a seedling.

terms.meaning: A careful guess about what will happen, with a reason, made before you test.
terms.example: I predict the dark seedlings will be smaller, because plants need light.
terms.art: A child writing in a notebook next to two cups.

terms.meaning: Units for measuring length. A centimetre is about the width of your fingernail. A millimetre is much smaller: 10 millimetres make 1 centimetre.
terms.example: A moong seedling 6 centimetres and 5 millimetres tall is 65 millimetres tall.
terms.art: A close-up of a ruler with the big centimetre lines and tiny millimetre lines.

terms.meaning: A neat table where you write what you measured, so nothing is forgotten.
terms.example: A table with a row for each cup and a column for each day.
terms.art: A notebook page with a hand-drawn table of numbers.

terms.meaning: A picture of numbers, with one bar for each thing. The taller the bar, the bigger the number.
terms.example: One bar for the light cup and one for the dark cup, as tall as their seedlings.
terms.art: A hand-drawn bar chart with two bars, one green and one yellow.

terms.meaning: What you found out, said in a sentence or two. It uses what you saw as proof.
terms.example: We found that seedlings in the dark grew tall, pale and floppy. This shows plants need light to grow well.
terms.art: A child reading out a sentence from a notebook.

terms.meaning: When a plant droops and goes floppy, usually because they do not have enough water.
terms.example: A tulsi plant left without water on a hot day wilts by the evening.
terms.art: A drooping plant beside a dry pot, then the same plant standing up after watering.

terms.meaning: When soil is so soaked that there is no air left in it. Roots in waterlogged soil cannot breathe.
terms.example: A pot standing in a full dish of water for a week becomes waterlogged.
terms.art: A pot standing in a deep dish of water, with sad yellow leaves.

terms.meaning: Tall, thin, pale and floppy, because a plant grew without enough light. Scientists call this etiolated.
terms.example: Moong grown in a dark cupboard comes out leggy and yellow.
terms.art: A tall, pale, bent seedling beside a short, green, strong one.

terms.meaning: The green substance in leaves that catches light. A plant makes it only when they get light.
terms.example: Leaves are green because of chlorophyll. Sprouts grown in a closed box are pale, because they have not made it yet.
terms.art: A leaf with a magnifier showing tiny green specks inside.

terms.meaning: The temperatures, or amounts of water or light, in which a kind of plant grows best. Below it or above it, the plant grows slowly or is harmed.
terms.example: Moong grows well between about 25 °C and 35 °C. Wheat likes it cooler.
terms.art: A thermometer with a green band in the middle and blue and red ends.

terms.meaning: A special molecule inside a plant that notices light. One kind, called phytochrome, also notices warmth.
terms.example: Photoreceptors tell a seedling under a box that it is dark.
terms.art: A cartoon molecule like a tiny switch, flipping when a sunbeam hits it.

terms.meaning: A tiny helper molecule inside living things that makes changes happen faster. Enzymes work faster when warm and slower when cold.
terms.example: Enzymes in a sprout help them use their stored food to grow.
terms.art: Tiny scissor-like helpers cutting and joining pieces inside a cell.

terms.meaning: A machine invented by Jagadish Chandra Bose in India. It made a plant's growth look thousands of times bigger, so you could see the plant grow minute by minute.
terms.example: Bose showed with it that a plant's growth speeds up and slows down when they are warmed, cooled or touched.
terms.art: An old brass machine with levers, a plant in a pot and a needle drawing a line on glass.

terms.meaning: Growing plants with their roots in water mixed with minerals, and no soil at all.
terms.example: Some farms on city rooftops grow lettuce in pipes of mineral water.
terms.art: Lettuce plants growing out of holes in a white pipe, their roots dangling in water.

explanations.definition: A plant needs light, water, air, warmth and minerals from the soil to live and grow well. They need each one in the right amount.
explanations.description: Think of everything you need to live: food, water, air and a place that is not too hot or too cold. A plant needs nearly the same things. But they do not eat food the way you do. They make their own food in their leaves, using light. That is why light is on their list. The soil gives the plant water, a few minerals and something to hold on to. The unit Food from light explains how the leaves make the food. The unit Plant parts shows which part does what.
examples: A tulsi pot on a sunny balcony, watered every morning, stays green and bushy.
Moong sprouts grown in a closed tiffin are pale. They have water and air, but no light.
A money plant in a jar of water grows for months with no soil at all, because the water carries a few minerals.
explanations.art: A happy plant in a pot surrounded by five small pictures: the Sun, a watering can, a breeze, a thermometer and a handful of soil.
explanations.context: This card gives the main idea of the whole unit: the list of things a plant needs.

explanations.concept: A fair test changes only one thing
explanations.definition: A fair test changes only one thing, called the variable, and keeps everything else the same. Then any difference in the results was caused by that one thing.
explanations.description: Imagine you put one cup of seedlings in a sunny window and another in a dark cupboard. But you also forget to water the cupboard cup. A week later the cupboard seedlings are dead. Was it the dark, or the thirst? You cannot tell, because two things changed. In a fair test you choose one thing to change. You keep everything else the same: the same kind of seeds, the same soil, the same cups and the same water. You measure the same way each time, and test more than one plant, because one plant can be a fluke.
examples: Light test: same seeds, same soil, same water. Only the light is different.
Water test: same seeds, same soil, same window. Only the amount of water is different.
Warmth test: same sprouts, same wet cotton, same dark boxes. Only the temperature is different.
explanations.art: Two identical paper cups of seedlings side by side with matching labels, the same spoon, the same soil bag, and one cardboard box over just one of them.
explanations.context: Scientists find out what a plant needs by testing. This card explains what makes a test fair, so its answer can be trusted.

explanations.concept: Light: why the dark seedling grows tall and yellow
explanations.definition: Without light, a seedling cannot make food or the green colour called chlorophyll. They use their stored food to grow tall and thin, searching for light. Scientists call this etiolation.
explanations.description: A seed carries a small store of food. A seedling in the light uses it to open green leaves quickly. Then the leaves catch light and make more food. A seedling in the dark cannot make food. So they spend their stored food on growing their stem as tall and as fast as they can, towards where light might be. They do not spend food on opening their leaves or making chlorophyll. That is why they end up tall, thin, yellow and floppy. When the stored food runs out, they die. Put them back in the light in time, and they start to turn green within a day. The chart shows made-up results from the light test.
examples: Moong in a dark cupboard grows taller than moong on a windowsill, but the plants are yellow and fall over.
Potatoes kept in a dark bag grow long, white, spidery shoots.
A plant in a dim corner leans towards the window and grows long gaps between their leaves.
explanations.art: Two seedlings side by side: a short dark-green one with open leaves in a sunbeam, and a tall, pale, hooked one in shadow, a measuring ruler between them.
explanations.context: Have you seen pale sprouts, or potato shoots from a dark basket? This card explains why plants grown in the dark come out tall, pale and floppy.

chart.title: The light test: made-up results after 7 days
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show the usual pattern. The dark seedlings are taller, but they are yellow, thin and floppy.

explanations.concept: Water: just right, not as much as possible
explanations.definition: A plant needs enough water to keep their cells full and firm, but not so much that their roots cannot get air. Too little water makes them wilt. Too much water makes their roots rot.
explanations.description: A plant is mostly water. Their tiny cells are full of water, like balloons full of air. The full cells push against each other, and that holds the leaves and soft stems up. With too little water, the cells go soft, like a balloon going flat, and the plant wilts. Water also carries minerals from the soil and is used to make food. But roots need air too. Root cells use oxygen from the air, just as your cells do. Soil has tiny air spaces between its grains. If the soil is always soaked, water fills every space. Then the roots cannot breathe, start to rot and turn brown, and the plant goes yellow. How water travels up a plant is in the unit How water moves up a plant.
examples: A tulsi left without water on a hot day wilts. After a good drink they stand up again within hours.
A pot standing in a dish of water for a week often has yellow leaves and soft, smelly roots.
Pots have a hole in the bottom so extra water can run out.
explanations.art: Three pots, a dry drooping plant, a happy green plant in damp soil and a yellow plant in soggy soil, with a zoom-in showing air spaces between soil grains in the middle pot.
explanations.context: People often think that more water is always better for a plant. This card explains why water must be just right.

explanations.concept: Warmth: growing faster, slower, or not at all
explanations.definition: Plants grow faster when they are warm and slower when they are cold. Too much heat harms them. Each kind of plant has a range of temperatures where they grow best.
explanations.description: Inside every living cell, tiny helpers called enzymes do the work of growing. They join and cut tiny pieces to build new cells. Enzymes work faster when they are warm, and very slowly when they are cold. So a plant in the cold hardly grows. They are not dead. They are waiting. Warm them up and they start again. But too much heat is harmful. The plant loses water fast and wilts. In great heat, the enzymes change shape and stop working, a bit like egg white turning solid in a hot pan. So for each kind of plant there is a best range of temperatures. Below it, growth is slow. Above it, the plant is harmed. The chart shows the usual pattern.
examples: Moong sprouts in a fridge hardly grow. Moved to a warm room, they start growing again.
In a hot May afternoon, many balcony plants droop, and then recover in the cool evening.
In the Himalayas, many plants only grow in the short warm summer.
explanations.art: A thermometer with three seedlings beside it: a tiny shivering one at the cold end, a tall happy one in the middle, and a drooping scorched one at the hot end.
explanations.context: Does warmth make a plant grow faster? This card explains how warmth helps, and how too much heat harms.

chart.title: How much moong sprouts grow in 3 days at different temperatures (a made-up example of the usual pattern)
chart.note: Made-up numbers. Growth rises with warmth, is best at around 30 to 35 degrees for moong, and falls when it is too hot. Never heat seeds at home above a warm room.

explanations.concept: Each kind of plant has their own just right
explanations.definition: Every kind of plant needs light, water and warmth, but each needs different amounts. These depend on the place their wild ancestors came from.
explanations.description: A cactus and a fern need very different amounts of water. A cactus lives in dry, sunny places and stores water in their fat stem. Water them every day and they rot. A fern lives in damp, shady places. Put them in full summer sun and their leaves burn. Indian farmers know this well. Wheat is sown at the start of the cool winter, and rice at the start of the hot, wet monsoon. Each crop is planted when the weather is just right for it.
examples: Aloe vera and cactus need only a little water. Money plant and ferns like more water and some shade.
Wheat grows in the cool winter in Punjab. Rice grows in the hot, wet monsoon.
Apples grow in cool hills like Himachal Pradesh. Coconuts grow on hot coasts like Kerala.
explanations.art: A row of plants each in their own home: a cactus in a desert, a fern by a waterfall, a wheat field in winter mist, rice in a flooded monsoon field.
explanations.context: Do all plants need the same things? This card explains that each kind of plant has their own just right.

explanations.concept: The shortest plank: the need in shortest supply
explanations.description: Imagine a wooden bucket made of planks, with one plank much shorter than the rest. Pour water in. It can only fill up to the top of the shortest plank. In the 1800s, two German scientists said plants are like this. A plant can only grow as well as their scarcest need allows. Give a plant more water when what they really lack is light, and they will not grow any better. Scientists still argue about how true this simple picture is.
examples: A plant in a dark corner will not grow better with extra fertiliser. Light is their shortest plank.
A farmer's field may have plenty of rain but very little nitrogen in the soil. Adding nitrogen helps more than adding water.

perspectives.who: Carl Sprengel, a German scientist, in 1828, and Justus von Liebig, another German scientist, around 1840
perspectives.explanation: A plant's growth is limited by whichever need is in shortest supply. Sprengel wrote this first. Liebig made it famous, and for a long time it was called Liebig's law of the minimum.

perspectives.who: Many plant scientists and ecologists today
perspectives.explanation: It is a useful rule, but too simple. Often two or three needs run short at the same time, and they affect each other. For example, a plant with more light may also need more water and minerals.

explanations.art: A wooden bucket with planks labelled light, water, warmth, air and minerals, with water spilling out over the shortest plank, labelled light.
explanations.context: Which need matters most? This card is about an old idea: that a plant grows only as well as their scarcest need allows.

explanations.concept: Measuring growth: watching a plant grow minute by minute
explanations.definition: To measure growth, measure the same thing, in the same way, at the same time, again and again. The difference between two measurements is how much the plant grew.
explanations.description: Plants grow too slowly for our eyes to see. So scientists measure them. You measure with a ruler, from the soil to the top of the plant, at the same time every day. Then you take away yesterday's height from today's height. The answer is how much the plant grew that day. More than a hundred years ago, in Kolkata, Jagadish Chandra Bose built a machine called the crescograph. It made a plant's growth look thousands of times bigger. A needle drew the growth as a line on a glass plate. Bose showed that growth is not steady. It speeds up and slows down from minute to minute, when the plant is warmed, cooled, touched or given a drop of chemical.
examples: A moong seedling might grow about 1 centimetre in a day. That is less than half a millimetre each hour.
Bamboo is one of the fastest growing plants. Some kinds can grow tens of centimetres in a day.
Cut a paper strip as tall as a seedling every day and stick the strips in a row. Each day's strip is a little longer.
explanations.art: Jagadish Chandra Bose in a Kolkata laboratory beside a brass crescograph, a needle tracing a wavy line on a smoked glass plate as a potted plant grows.
explanations.context: How do we see something that is too slow to see? This card is about measuring a plant's growth, from a school ruler to Jagadish Chandra Bose's growth machine.

explanations.definition: Temperature tells how fast the tiny molecules in something are moving. Warmer molecules move faster and bump into each other more often, so the work of growing goes faster. But too much heat breaks the plant's helper molecules.
explanations.description: Everything is made of tiny pieces called molecules, far too small to see. They are always moving. When something is warm, its molecules move faster. When it is cold, they move slowly. Inside a plant, enzymes are the tiny helpers that build new cells. They work when other molecules bump into them and get joined or cut. In the warm, more bumps happen each second, so growing goes faster. In the cold, bumps are rare, so growing almost stops. But each enzyme is folded into a special shape. Too much heat shakes it so hard that it unfolds and stops working. That is why great heat harms a plant.
examples: Sugar dissolves faster in hot water than in cold water, because the hot water's molecules move faster and bump into the sugar more.
An egg white turns solid and white when cooked, because heat unfolds its molecules. It never turns back.
explanations.art: A zoom from a moong sprout into a cell, then to tiny moving balls bumping into a folded ribbon-shaped enzyme, slow and blue in the cold, fast and red in the warm.
explanations.context: This card zooms in, far past anything a microscope can show, to see why warmth makes plants grow faster.

explanations.concept: How does a plant know they are in the dark, or the warm?
explanations.description: A plant has no eyes and no skin like ours. But they have special molecules called photoreceptors that notice light. One family of them is called phytochrome. It works like a tiny switch. Red light flips it one way. Darkness, and the deep red light that filters through other leaves, slowly flips it back. So a seedling can tell if they are in the light, in the dark, or in the shade of other plants. In 2016, two teams of scientists found something surprising. Phytochrome flips back faster when it is warm. So the same molecule is a light sensor and a thermometer. Scientists think plants have other warmth sensors too. How they all work together is still being worked out.
examples: A seedling under a box senses that it is dark, and grows tall towards where light might be.
A plant in the shade of taller plants senses the changed light, and stretches up to get out of their shade.

perspectives.who: Two teams of plant scientists in 2016. One was led by Philip Wigge in Cambridge, England. One was led by Jorge Casal in Buenos Aires, Argentina.
perspectives.explanation: They found that phytochrome B, a light-sensing molecule, also changes faster when it is warm. So it helps the plant feel temperature.
They have found more molecules in plants that change when it gets warm. Plants seem to use several sensors together. Which ones matter most, in which plants, is still open.

explanations.art: A tiny cartoon switch inside a leaf cell: a red sunbeam flips it ON, a dark night slowly flips it OFF, and a little thermometer beside it shows that warmth speeds up the flip back.
explanations.context: Plants have no eyes and no brain. This card is about how they still notice light and warmth, and what scientists are still finding out.

explanations.definition: Plants do not need soil itself. They need what soil gives them: support, water, air for the roots and minerals. Growing plants in mineral water without soil is called hydroponics.
explanations.description: Most plants grow in soil, so it is easy to think they need it. But think about what soil gives a plant. It holds the roots, so the plant does not fall over. It holds water, with air between its grains. And it has small amounts of minerals. If you give a plant those things another way, they do not need soil at all. In the 1860s, two German scientists, Julius Sachs and Wilhelm Knop, grew plants with their roots in water mixed with minerals. In the 1930s, an American scientist, William Gericke, grew huge tomato plants this way and called it hydroponics. Many city farms in India now grow lettuce and herbs like this.
examples: A money plant cutting grows roots and leaves in a jar of water on a windowsill.
Rooftop farms grow lettuce in plastic pipes of mineral water.
Plants grow out of cracks in walls and temple towers, with only a little dust and rainwater.
explanations.art: A money plant in a glass jar of water beside a plant in soil, with arrows showing that both get water, air, minerals and support.
explanations.context: Most plants grow in soil. This card asks whether soil itself is a need, or only what soil gives.

explanations.definition: Plants use light from the Sun. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to travel from the Sun to the Earth.
explanations.description: The light falling on a leaf on your windowsill comes from the Sun, a star. It left the Sun about 8 minutes ago and crossed 150 million kilometres of empty space. Its energy was made deep in the Sun's centre, where hydrogen particles crash together and join. This is called nuclear fusion. That energy spent tens of thousands of years, or more, working its way out from the centre before it flew off as light. Only a tiny part of the sunlight that reaches the Earth is caught by leaves. But that tiny part feeds nearly every living thing, including you. When you eat an idli, you are eating sunlight that a rice plant caught.
examples: A leaf in the morning catches light that left the Sun only 8 minutes earlier.
The energy in your breakfast came from sunlight caught by a plant.
explanations.art: A beam of light travelling from the glowing Sun across black space to a moong seedling on an Indian windowsill, a clock showing 8 minutes along the way.
explanations.context: This card follows the light that a plant needs all the way back to where it came from.

explanations.concept: Plants in space and on the Moon
explanations.definition: To grow plants away from Earth, people must give them everything Earth gives for free. That means light, water, moving air, the right warmth and minerals.
explanations.description: Astronauts on long journeys will need to grow food. So scientists test what plants need away from Earth. On the International Space Station there is a small garden called Veggie. It gives plants mostly red and blue light from lamps, with a little green, and water through soft pillows. A fan moves the air, because in space warm air does not rise. In August 2015, astronauts there ate red lettuce they had grown themselves. In January 2019, a Chinese spacecraft called Chang'e 4 carried cotton seeds to the far side of the Moon in a sealed can. A cotton seed sprouted, the first ever on the Moon. But the freezing Moon night arrived, and the experiment ended. In 2022, scientists in Florida grew small plants in real Moon soil brought back by Apollo astronauts. The plants grew, but slowly, and they showed signs of stress.
examples: The Veggie garden on the space station lights its lettuce with mostly red and blue lamps, which give a pink glow.
Cotton sprouted on the Moon in 2019, but could not survive the freezing Moon night.
Plants grown in real Moon soil in 2022 were smaller than the same plants grown in volcanic ash from Earth, which is often used to copy Moon soil.
explanations.art: Inside a space station, an astronaut holding a small leaf of red lettuce growing under pink-purple lamps, Earth in the window behind.
explanations.context: Could plants grow in space? This card is about what happened when people tried, which shows very clearly what plants need.

explanations.concept: Do plants grow better with music or talking?
explanations.description: Many people say their plants grow better when they talk or sing to them. Some books have said so too. Scientists ask: was the test fair? A person who talks to their plants usually also visits them more, waters them more carefully and notices problems sooner. They also breathe out a little carbon dioxide and moist air near the leaves. So more than one thing changes. A fair test would need two groups of plants treated exactly the same, except for the sound.
examples: Some people play music to plants in their greenhouses.
A plant that is talked to every day probably also gets watered and checked every day.

perspectives.who: Some gardeners and a few popular books, such as The Sound of Music and Plants by Dorothy Retallack, in 1973
perspectives.explanation: Plants grow better with gentle music and worse with loud rock music.
Those tests were small and not fair enough. Other things changed too. Careful tests have not shown that music makes plants grow better.

perspectives.who: Heidi Appel and Rex Cocroft, two scientists in the USA, in 2014
perspectives.explanation: Plants do respond to some vibrations. They shook the leaves of thale cress, a small weed that scientists often study, with a recording of the vibrations caterpillars make when they chew. Later, when real caterpillars fed on these plants, the plants made more of their bitter defence chemicals. So plants can sense some sounds, but this is not the same as liking music.

explanations.art: A child singing to a tulsi plant, with small question marks floating above: music? care? water? breath?
explanations.context: Many people believe plants like music. This card looks at what scientists have found, and why it is hard to test fairly.

agreed.text: Plants need light, water, air, suitable warmth and minerals to grow well.
agreed.evidence: Farmers and gardeners have seen this for thousands of years. Scientists have tested each need with fair tests, taking it away and keeping everything else the same.
agreed.context: This card is about the needs of plants that nearly all scientists agree on.

agreed.text: Seedlings grown in the dark grow tall, thin and pale, and die when their stored food runs out.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can repeat the light test with moong in a week. The pale colour is because plants make chlorophyll only in light.
agreed.context: This card is about what happens to plants in the dark.

chart.title: The light test: made-up results after 7 days
chart.y: Open green leaves on the 3 tallest seedlings
chart.note: Made-up numbers. Each light seedling had 2 open green leaves. The dark seedlings were taller, but they had no open green leaves.

agreed.text: Roots need air. Waterlogged soil harms most plants.
agreed.evidence: Roots kept in soaked soil turn brown and rot. Some plants do live in water, like rice, lotus and the mangroves of the Sundarbans. They have special air channels or breathing roots that carry air down.
agreed.context: This card is about why too much water is harmful.

agreed.text: Plants grow faster when warm and slower when cold, and each kind of plant has their own best range of temperature.
agreed.evidence: Growth has been measured at different temperatures in many experiments. Farmers sow each crop in the season that suits it.
agreed.context: This card is about warmth and plant growth.

agreed.text: We can only trust a test of what plants need if it changes one thing and uses more than one plant.
agreed.evidence: When scientists repeat careful fair tests in different places, they get the same answers. Unfair tests give answers that do not repeat.
agreed.context: This card is about why scientists insist on fair tests.

challenging.claim: The more water you give a plant, the better they grow.
challenging.who: A very common idea, especially among people who love their plants
challenging.for: Plants wilt and die without water. So it seems that more must be better.
challenging.against: Roots need air. In always-soaked soil, water fills the air spaces, the roots cannot breathe and they rot. Gardeners often say that more house plants die from too much water than from too little.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea of how to look after a plant.

challenging.claim: A taller seedling is a healthier seedling.
challenging.who: Many of us, without thinking about it
challenging.for: Healthy plants do grow. Height is easy to measure and compare.
challenging.against: In the dark, seedlings grow tallest of all, because they are stretching to find light. They are pale, thin and floppy. Health shows in green colour, firm stems and open leaves as well as height.
challenging.context: This card is about how we judge whether a plant is doing well.

challenging.claim: Plants get their food from the soil.
challenging.who: Most people, for most of history
challenging.for: Plants grow in soil, and dry soil or poor soil gives poor plants.
challenging.against: In the 1600s, Jan Baptist van Helmont, a scientist in what is now Belgium, grew a willow tree in a pot for 5 years. The tree gained about 74 kilograms, but the soil lost only about 57 grams. The plant makes their food in their leaves, from light, air and water. The unit Food from light tells this story.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of where a plant's food comes from.

challenging.for: Almost all the plants we see grow in soil.
challenging.against: A money plant grows in a jar of water. Hydroponic farms grow lettuce in mineral water, and astronauts grew lettuce in space in soft pillows. Plants need what soil gives, not soil itself.
challenging.context: This card asks whether soil is a need, or only a helper.

challenging.claim: Justus von Liebig discovered that a plant grows only as well as their scarcest need allows.
challenging.who: Many older textbooks, which call it Liebig's law of the minimum
challenging.for: Liebig, a famous German scientist, wrote about it around 1840 and made the idea famous around the world.
challenging.against: Carl Sprengel, a less famous German scientist, published the idea in 1828, about twelve years earlier. Historians now often call it the Sprengel and Liebig law of the minimum.
challenging.context: This card is about who gets the credit for an important idea about what plants need.

challenging.claim: Plants grow better if you talk or sing to them.
challenging.who: Many gardeners, and some popular books
challenging.for: Many people say their talked-to plants do well.
challenging.against: Talking usually comes with more care, more watering and more checking, so the test is not fair. Careful fair tests have not shown that music helps growth, though plants can sense some vibrations.
challenging.context: This card is about a popular belief about plants and sound.

big_questions.q: A seedling in the dark grows tall instead of green. Is that a mistake, or a clever plan?
big_questions.hint: Imagine you are in a dark tunnel with your last packed lunch. You see a crack of light far above. What would you do?

big_questions.q: Why can't a plant just walk to the light, or to water, as an animal can? How do they cope instead?
big_questions.hint: Watch how a plant on a windowsill leans, and how roots spread. Plants move by growing.

big_questions.q: In the water test, the moong standing in water had the most water, but they did worse than the moong given a spoonful a day. Is more always better?
big_questions.hint: Think of the cups standing in water. What else is good in the right amount, but harmful when there is too much?

big_questions.q: The same moong seeds grew short and green in the light, and tall and pale in the dark. Which one shows what a moong plant really looks like?
big_questions.hint: Is there one true shape, or does the shape always depend on where they grow? Think about how your skin changes in strong sun.

big_questions.q: The Buddha taught a middle path, between too much and too little. Plants seem to live on a middle path too. Where else in life is the middle the best place to be?
big_questions.hint: Think about food, sleep, screen time, and how hard to push a friend on a swing.

big_questions.q: In our light test, we kept some seedlings in the dark until they were weak. Is it fair to the plants? When is it right to do experiments on living things?
big_questions.hint: What do we learn? Can we give the dark plants back their light at the end? Would you test on an animal?

big_questions.q: The light that grew your idli left the Sun about 8 minutes before the rice plant caught it. So are you made of sunlight?
big_questions.hint: Follow your food back step by step: idli, batter, rice plant, leaf, sunlight.

big_questions.q: If people one day live on the Moon or Mars, what will they need to bring for plants, that Earth gives for free?
big_questions.hint: Make a list: light, air, water, warmth, minerals. Which ones does the Moon have?

big_questions.q: Carl Sprengel had an idea first, but Justus von Liebig made it famous. Who should get the credit for an idea: the person who has it first, or the person who spreads it?
big_questions.hint: Has someone ever said your idea louder than you, and got the praise?

big_questions.q: A plant cannot tell us in words what they need. How can we listen to something that does not use words?
big_questions.hint: A plant doctor reads clues: drooping, yellow, leaning. A baby cannot use words either. How do people find out what a baby needs?

story.title: A Stripe of Sun
story.note: Zoya, Nani, Rukmini Mami, Arjun and the contest are made up. What happens to Zoya's moong is real: you can see it in this unit's light test.
text: In Zoya's lane in Triplicane, in Chennai, the buildings stood very close together. Neighbours could pass a bowl of kesari from one balcony to the next without leaning. Sunlight reached the lane for only about an hour each day. At eleven o'clock a thin yellow stripe slid down the wall opposite Zoya's window. For a while it touched the outer edge of the iron grille around her window. Then it was gone before lunch.

In the May holidays, Rukmini Mami from the ground floor made an announcement on the staircase. Every child in the building would get a paper cup of soil and five moong beans from her own kitchen. In two weeks there would be judging, right there on the landing. 'The tallest plant wins,' she said. She held up a mango so ripe that it smelt like a festival. 'A Malgova, from Salem. One.'

Arjun from the fourth floor carried his cup up to the terrace, where the sun beat down all day long. Kavitha's mother put hers on the kitchen window, next to the pressure cooker. Zoya put hers on her own windowsill, between Nani's spectacles case and a jar of buttons, facing the wall.

On the third day, two pale loops pushed up through Zoya's soil, like the handles of tiny bags. By the fifth day the loops had straightened and shot up past the rim of the cup. Zoya measured them every evening with her school ruler, from the soil to the very top. She wrote the numbers on the back of an old calendar. Four centimetres. Seven. Ten and a half.

Every evening she climbed to the terrace to look at Arjun's cup. His plants were short. They were hardly past the rim. 'Mine is winning,' she told Nani, who sat by the window every afternoon doing the crossword. 'Hm,' said Nani. That was what she said when she did not agree, but wanted you to find out for yourself.

Arjun's moong was short, but the plants were thick, and dark green. Each stem held up two round leaves, open flat like hands waiting for something to be put into them. Zoya's moong was tall, but the plants were a pale, washed-out yellow-green. Their leaves were small and only half open. And every stem leaned the same way, towards the window, as if they were listening for a voice outside.

On the eighth day, Zoya came home from her cousin's house and found her tallest plant lying across the rim of the cup. Nobody had knocked them. They had simply folded, like a tired arm. She stood them up and leaned them against a pencil. In the morning, two more had fallen.

At eleven o'clock the stripe of sun arrived on the wall opposite. Zoya was sitting with her chin on the windowsill when it came, so she saw. The plants did not move, or not that she could see. But for the first time she noticed exactly where they were pointing. They pointed at the bright stripe. All of them, like people on a railway platform leaning out to look down the line for the train. They had been pointing at it all along.

Zoya looked at her calendar of numbers. Four, seven, ten and a half, fourteen, eighteen. They did not look like winning numbers any more. They looked like someone running. Running and running down a long dark corridor towards a door far away, spending everything they had. Each moong bean had carried a little food inside, enough to get started. Arjun's plants had spent theirs on opening green leaves, and then the sun had fed them. Hers had never found enough sun. So they had spent every crumb on getting taller.

Zoya went into the kitchen and came back with Ammi's biggest steel thali, the one kept for guests. She leaned out to the edge of the grille, where the stripe of sun touched it, and tilted the thali. A bright, wobbly circle of light landed on the windowsill. It slid across the buttons, and onto the cup. 'Ammi will want that back by dinner,' said Nani, without looking up. But she put down her pen and held the thali steady while Zoya tied it to the grille with string.

That afternoon, Zoya sowed five more moong in a second cup and set it where the circle of light fell. Every day at eleven she turned the thali a little, to follow the sun. It was like turning the pages of a slow book.

On judging day, eleven cups stood in a row on the landing. Rukmini Mami walked along them with her tailor's tape. Zoya's first cup was still the tallest, even propped on their pencil: nineteen centimetres. Arjun's was nine. Kavitha's had got too hot next to the cooker and given up. 'Zoya!' said Rukmini Mami, and held out the mango.

Zoya did not take it. Her face was burning. 'They are tall because they are hungry,' she said. Everyone looked at her. She tried again. 'This is not the best plant. This is the plant that was looking hardest. Arjun's is the one that found what they were looking for.'

Rukmini Mami looked at the yellow plant leaning on their pencil for a long time. Then she looked at Arjun's, short and green and stubborn. She rolled up her tape. 'Then next year,' she said slowly, 'I will need a better ruler.'

Arjun got the mango. He cut it on the terrace, and the juice ran down eleven chins. But Zoya hardly tasted her slice. She was thinking of the second cup on her windowsill downstairs. Its plants were only as tall as her little finger. They were green as a parrot. And they were leaning, every one of them, towards an old steel thali full of sun.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Zoya's plant grew tallest because they were starving for light. A seedling in dim light spends their stored food on stretching their stem, and stays pale with folded leaves. Scientists call this etiolation. So height alone is the wrong measure of how well a plant is doing. Light was the need in shortest supply, and Zoya fixed it by bouncing sunlight in with a thali. The story also asks what we choose to measure, and whether the person with the biggest number has really done best.
ask: Zoya's moong grew the tallest. Why weren't they the healthiest?
Which way were all Zoya's plants leaning? What were they looking for?
How did the steel thali help the second cup of moong?
Rukmini Mami said she would need 'a better ruler' next year. What else could she measure, to find the healthiest plant?
Have you ever won, or lost, because of the wrong kind of measuring? For example, the most marks but not the best understanding?

rules: Each player is a moong seedling. Put your counter on square 1 and take 4 green leaf tokens and 2 rescue cards.
Shuffle the weather and care cards and put them face down.
On your turn, take the top card, read it out and do what it says.
You may play a rescue card when a card says so. To play it, say which need it gives back to your plant. It might be light, water, air for the roots, the right warmth or space.
Cupboard and doormat cards move you up fast, but you lose a green leaf. Tall and pale is not the same as healthy.
To win, reach square 20 with at least one green leaf token left. A seedling with no leaves left must go back to square 1 and start again with 2 leaves.

flow.do: 1. Put the board in the middle. 2. Give each player a counter, 4 leaf tokens and 2 rescue cards. 3. Shuffle the weather and care cards and put them face down.
flow.say: You are all moong seedlings. To flower, you need light, water, air, the right warmth and space. But watch out. Some cards make you grow fast and pale, and others drown you.
flow.kid: You are a moong seedling. Put your counter on the seed. Take 4 leaf tokens and 2 rescue cards. Try to reach the flower with at least one leaf.
flow.context: This is the first step of Grow or Droop. It is a race game about what plants need. Each player is a seedling trying to grow from a seed to a flower.

flow.do: Play the card 'The pot stood in a dish of water all week' together as a practice round.
flow.say: Let's practise with one card. The pot stood in a dish of water all week. Is that good or bad for the plant? Why?
flow.kid: Practice card: the pot stood in water all week. Good or bad for the plant? Tap your answer.

ask.q: Why does standing in water harm the plant?
good: The soil is soaked, so the roots can't get air.

check.q: The pot stood in a dish of water all week. What happens to the roots?
options: They get lots of water, so the plant grows faster
They cannot get air, so they start to rot
check.why: Roots need air as well as water. In soaked soil, water fills the tiny air spaces, so the roots cannot breathe. They go brown and soft. Picking 'grows faster' usually means thinking more water is always better. The Drainage Hole card fixes this, because extra water runs out.

flow.do: 1. Take turns drawing and reading cards. 2. When a player plays a rescue card, they must name the need it gives back. 3. When a TEST IT card comes up, everyone does it together.
flow.say: When you play a rescue card, tell us which need it gives back to your plant.
flow.kid: Take turns. Read your card out loud. Do what it says. If you play a rescue card, say which need it gives back.
flow.parent: Good answers: Watering Can gives water. Drainage Hole lets extra water out, so roots get air. Shade protects from too much heat. Move to the Light gives light. Bigger Pot gives roots space. Notice who rushes up with the cupboard cards and then runs out of leaves. That is the lesson of the light test.

flow.do: When someone draws a cupboard or doormat card, stop for a moment and ask the question below.
flow.say: This card moved you up 3 squares. So why did you lose a leaf?
flow.kid: You grew fast in the cupboard, but lost a leaf. Why? Say it out loud.

ask.q: Why does a seedling in the dark grow fast but lose their leaves?
good: They can't make green colour or food without light.
Tall isn't the same as healthy.

flow.think: If you could only measure one thing to judge a plant, what would you choose? Height, leaves, or colour?

flow.do: Find the winner. Then lay out every card that pushed someone back, and sort them by which need was missing.
flow.say: Look at the cards that hurt our plants. Which need was missing each time: light, water, air, warmth or space?
flow.kid: Who won? Now look at the cards that sent you back. Which need was missing each time?
flow.think: Which cards were about too little of something? Which were about too much?

items.f: A girl puts one moong cup in the sun and one in a cupboard. She waters both with 2 spoons a day.
A girl puts one moong cup in the sun and one in a cupboard. She forgets to water the cupboard cup.
items.b: UNFAIR. Water changed too. Fix: water both cups the same.

items.f: A girl tests if plants need water. She uses a tiny seedling with no water and a big plant with water.
items.b: UNFAIR. The size of the plant changed. Fix: use two seedlings of the same size.

items.f: A girl grows 3 cups with water every day and 3 cups with no water, all on the same windowsill.
A boy puts methi in the fridge and moong in a warm room to see if warmth matters.
items.b: UNFAIR. The kind of seed changed. Fix: use the same seed in both.

items.f: A girl puts 10 sprouts in the fridge, 10 in a cupboard and 10 on top of the fridge, all in closed dark boxes.
A girl measures her light cup in the morning and her dark cup at night.
items.b: UNFAIR. The time of measuring changed. Fix: measure both cups at the same time.

items.f: A girl measures every cup at 6 o'clock every evening, from the soil to the top of the tallest seedling.
items.b: FAIR. Every cup is measured the same way, at the same time.

items.f: A girl tests soil from the garden against soil from a shop. She also uses a bigger pot for the shop soil.
items.b: UNFAIR. The pot size changed. Fix: use the same size of pot.

items.f: A boy grows one seed in the sun and one seed in the shade, then says the sun is better.
items.b: NOT TO BE TRUSTED. Only one seed in each place, so the result could be a fluke. Fix: use many seeds in each place.

items.f: A girl uses the same spoon to water every cup, and fills it to the brim each time.
items.b: FAIR. Every cup gets the same water.

items.f: A girl tests music on her plants. The music plant is in her bedroom window. The quiet plant is in the bathroom.
items.b: UNFAIR. The light and the warmth changed too. Fix: put both plants in the same place.

items.f: A girl tests green cellophane and clear cellophane over two cups. Both cups are the same, side by side.
items.b: FAIR. Only the colour of the cellophane changes.

items.f: A boy waters his sunny plant with tap water and his shady plant with fridge water.
items.b: UNFAIR. The water temperature changed too. Fix: use tap water for both.

items.f: A girl plants the same moong seeds in the same soil, in the same cups, and only changes how much water.
items.b: FAIR. Only the amount of water changes.

items.f: A girl tests warmth with one box in the fridge and one box on a sunny windowsill without a lid.
items.b: UNFAIR. The light and the lid changed too. Fix: give both boxes a lid and the same light.

printables.title: Two paddles to hold up
items: FAIR ✅
UNFAIR ❌

rules: Shuffle the 16 test cards and put them face down.
One player reads the front of a test card out loud.
Everyone holds up a paddle at the same time: FAIR or UNFAIR. Then turn the card over to check.
If it is unfair, the first player to name the extra thing that changed wins a token.
A second token goes to anyone who says how to fix the test, so only one thing changes.
After all the cards, the player with the most tokens is the Chief Fair Tester.

flow.do: 1. Shuffle the test cards. 2. Give each player a FAIR and an UNFAIR paddle. 3. Put the tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: A fair test changes only one thing. Everything else stays the same. Each card tells us about a test a child did. Your job is to spot the unfair ones.
flow.kid: Each card is a test a child did. Is it fair? A fair test changes only one thing. Hold up your answer.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fair or Unfair?, a game about fair tests. A fair test changes only one thing and keeps everything else the same.

flow.do: Read the card about the forgotten watering together as a practice round.
flow.say: A girl puts one moong cup in the sun and one in a cupboard. She forgets to water the cupboard cup. Fair or unfair?
flow.kid: A girl puts one cup in the sun and one in a cupboard. She forgets to water the cupboard cup. Fair or unfair?

check.q: A girl puts one cup in the sun and one in a cupboard. She forgets to water the cupboard cup. Is it a fair test of light?
options: Fair, because she changed the light
Unfair, because the light and the water both changed
check.why: Two things changed: light and water. If the cupboard seedlings die, she cannot tell which one caused it. To fix it, she waters both cups the same. Picking 'fair' usually means noticing the thing that was changed on purpose, but not the thing that changed by accident.

flow.do: 1. Take turns reading the cards. 2. Everyone holds up a paddle together. 3. Give tokens for naming the extra change, and for a good fix.
flow.say: Paddles up! If it's unfair, what else changed? How would you fix it?
flow.kid: Paddles up! If it is unfair, say what else changed. Then say how to fix it.
flow.parent: The fair ones are the cards where only one thing changes: the cups both watered, 3 cups with water and 3 without, the three places for the sprouts, measuring every cup at the same time, the same spoon for every cup, the two cellophanes, and only the amount of water. The unfair ones are these. The forgotten watering changed water too. The tiny seedling against the big plant changed plant size. Methi against moong changed the kind of seed. Morning against night changed the time of measuring. The bigger pot changed pot size. The one seed in the sun and one in the shade used only one seed each, so the result could be a fluke. The music test changed light and warmth. The fridge water changed water temperature. The box without a lid changed light and the lid as well as warmth. The one-seed test is a good one to argue about. Only one seed is not exactly unfair, but it cannot be trusted.

flow.do: Finish with the scoring, then ask the closing question.
flow.say: Why do scientists care so much about changing only one thing?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Who is the Chief Fair Tester? Why do scientists change only one thing?

ask.q: Why do scientists change only one thing at a time?
good: So they know what caused the result.
If two things change, you can't tell which one did it.

flow.think: When something goes wrong at home, like milk going sour, how could you find out the cause with a fair test?

items.p: A girl keeps a cup of moong seedlings under an upside-down cardboard box for a week. She waters them just like her other cup. What will they look like when she lifts the box?
opts: Short and dark green
Tall, thin and pale yellow, with small folded leaves
Exactly the same as the seedlings in the light
items.why: In the dark, a seedling spends their stored food on stretching up to find light. They cannot make green chlorophyll without light, so they stay pale. Picking 'short and dark green' means guessing that the dark only slows a plant down. In fact the dark makes them grow taller, but weaker.
items.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.

items.p: Many people think the tallest plant is the healthiest. In the light test, the dark seedlings grew tallest. Why were they not the healthiest?
items.a: They were tall only because they were stretching to find light. They were pale, thin and floppy, with small folded leaves, and some fell over. The short seedlings in the light were green, with open leaves and strong stems.
items.why: A strong answer uses what the child saw: colour, leaves and stem, not only height. Height alone can fool you.

The cupboard sprouts
items.why: Cold slows down the work of growing. The fridge is about 5 °C and a kitchen cupboard is about 27 °C, so the cupboard sprouts grow much more. Picking 'both the same' means thinking that only light and water matter.
items.context: This question is about the warmth test. Moong sprouts are kept in the dark in a fridge, a room cupboard and a warm spot, and measured each day.

items.p: In the warmth test, the fridge is dark inside. Why do we cover the cupboard bowl and the warm bowl with plates too?
items.a: So all three bowls are in the dark. Then the only thing that is different is how warm they are. If only the fridge bowl was dark, both light and warmth would change, and we could not tell which one made the difference.
items.why: A strong answer says the plates keep the light the same, so warmth is the only thing that changes.
items.context: This question is about the warmth test. Moong sprouts are kept in the dark in a fridge, a room cupboard and a warm spot, and measured each day.

items.p: Draw two seedlings: one grown in the light and one grown in the dark. Label three differences.
items.a: The light seedling is short, thick and green, with open leaves. The dark seedling is tall, thin and pale yellow, bent over, with tiny folded leaves.
items.why: A strong drawing labels colour, leaves and stem, not only height.
items.art: An empty box split in two halves, labelled LIGHT and DARK.
items.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.

items.p: It is May in Chennai. Lakshmi, a girl of 8, her grandmother and her mother disagree about how to water the tulsi plant on their sunny balcony.

views.says: Water the tulsi every morning and every evening. In this heat the soil dries out fast.
Water only when the top of the soil feels dry. Too much water stops the roots getting air.
Keep a saucer of water under the pot all the time. Then the plant can drink whenever they need to.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from the tests in this unit. Then say one thing that another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and backs it with evidence. Lakshmi's finger test works in every season, and the SOAKED cups showed that too much water harms roots. A strong answer also gives others their due. Paati is right that a pot in the Chennai sun may really need water twice a day. Amma's saucer is fine if it is emptied, but kept full it soaks the soil like the SOAKED cups.
items.why: There is a real trade-off. Too little water and too much water both harm a plant, and the right amount changes with the weather. Checking the soil is a way to find the right amount each day.

items.p: A girl measures her moong seedling from the rim of the cup, not from the soil. What goes wrong?
opts: Her numbers are too big
Her numbers are too small, because she misses the part of the stem inside the cup
Nothing goes wrong
items.why: The soil is lower than the rim. Measuring from the rim leaves out the bottom of the stem, so every height is too small. A plant's height is measured from the soil to their highest point.

items.p: When a plant droops and goes floppy because they have too little water, we say the plant ____.
items.why: A plant's cells are firm when full of water, like a blown-up balloon. Without water they go soft, and the plant droops.

items.p: A girl grows one cup of moong in the light and one cup in the dark. Her teacher says she should grow 3 cups of each. Why?
opts: One cup can be a fluke, for example if the seeds in it were bad
Three cups are easier to water
One cup is not fair to the seeds
items.why: If one cup does something odd, you cannot tell whether it was the light or just bad luck. With 3 cups you can see if they all do the same thing. Then you use the middle result.
items.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.

items.p: A plant's roots need air, as well as water.
items.why: True. Roots breathe in air from the tiny spaces in the soil. That is why the SOAKED cups, with no air spaces left, turned yellow and rotted.

items.p: A plant can grow without any soil, if their roots get water and minerals.
items.why: True. A money plant grows in a jar of water. Plants need what the soil gives them, water and minerals, not the soil itself.

items.p: Your plant is drooping and their soil is dry. Your friend's plant is also drooping, but their soil is wet and smells bad. Should you both water your plants? Explain.
items.a: I should water mine, because dry soil means they are short of water. My friend should not. Wet, smelly soil means the roots have too much water and no air, and they are starting to rot. My friend should let the soil dry out and check that the pot has a hole.
items.why: The same clue, drooping, can have two opposite causes. A strong answer looks at the soil before deciding.

items.p: You want to test if plants need light. Which test is fair?
opts: One pot in the sun with water, and one pot in a cupboard with no water
A big plant in the sun and a tiny plant in the cupboard
Two pots of the same seedlings and soil, both watered the same, one in the sun and one in a cupboard
items.why: Only the light is different in this test. The sun-and-no-water choice misses that water changed too. The big-and-tiny choice misses that the plants were different sizes.

items.p: Rice plants stand in water in flooded fields. Why don't their roots rot, like our soaked moong?
opts: Rice roots don't need air
Rice plants have air channels that carry air down to their roots
The water in rice fields is special
items.why: Rice, lotus and mangroves all have ways to get air down to their roots. Moong does not. 'Rice roots don't need air' is a common guess, but all roots need air. Rice plants have their own air pipes.

items.p: A boy waters his cactus every day, like his other plants. After a few weeks, the cactus stem goes soft and black at the bottom. What happened?
opts: The roots rotted from too much water, because a cactus needs very little
The cactus got too little water
The cactus needed more sun
items.why: A cactus comes from dry places and needs only a little water. Daily watering drowns their roots. Picking 'too little water' means using one rule for every plant. Each kind of plant has their own just right.

items.p: Plan a fair test to find out if methi grows better in sunlight or in a shady corner. Say what you will change, what you will keep the same, and what you will measure.
items.a: I will change only the place: 3 cups of methi in the sun and 3 cups in the shade. I will keep the same seeds, soil, cups and water. Every two days I will measure the tallest seedling in each cup and count the green leaves.
items.why: A strong plan names one thing to change, several things to keep the same, and what to measure. It uses more than one cup in each place.

items.p: Draw a bar chart of the water test results: NONE 5 cm, JUST RIGHT 13 cm, SOAKED 8 cm. Label the bottom line and the side line.
items.a: Three bars. NONE is 5 squares tall, JUST RIGHT is 13 and SOAKED is 8. The bottom line says 'Group' and the side line says 'Height (cm)'.
items.why: A bar chart shows at a glance which group grew best.
items.art: Empty squared graph paper with a bottom line and a side line numbered 0 to 15.
items.context: This question is about the water test. Three cups of moong get no water. Three get 1 tablespoon of water every morning. Three stand in a dish of water all the time.

items.p: Usha, a girl in Class 4, says: 'My plant grows well because I talk to them every day.' What is the best question to ask her?
opts: What do you say to your plant?
Is it a big plant?
Do you also water and check that plant more than your other plants?
items.why: Talking to a plant usually comes with more care, so more than one thing changes. Picking 'what do you say' takes it for granted that talking is the cause, before anyone has tested it.

items.p: Is this a need that a plant has, or something they can live without?
items: light
A need
warmth
A need
water
A need
music
Can live without
air for their roots
A need
fertiliser from a shop
Can live without
items.a: see items
items.why: Plants need light, warmth, water, air and minerals. Minerals can come from soil or compost, so shop fertiliser is a help, not a need. Music has not been shown to help plants grow.

items.p: You measured your three cups in the light: 8 cm, 9 cm and 8 cm. What is the middle value?
opts: 9 cm
8 cm
25 cm
items.why: Put them in order: 8, 8, 9. The middle one is 8. Picking 25 means adding them all up. The middle value is one of the numbers, not their total.
items.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.

items.p: In Ooty, high up in the Nilgiri hills, farmers grow lots of carrots and cabbages. In hot Chennai, few people grow them. Why?
opts: Carrots and cabbages grow best in cool weather, and Ooty is cool because it is high up
Ooty soil is the only soil carrots like
Chennai has no water for farms
items.why: Each kind of plant has their own just-right warmth. High places are cooler, so the Nilgiris suit cool-weather crops. Picking 'soil' misses that warmth is one of a plant's needs.

items.p: In the story, Rukmini Mami promised a mango to the child with the tallest moong. Zoya's moong was the tallest, but pale and falling over. Arjun's was short and dark green.

views.who: Rukmini Mami, who ran the contest
views.says: The rule was 'the tallest plant wins'. Everyone knew it from the start, so Zoya should win.
My moong is tall only because they were starving for light. Arjun's moong is the healthiest, so he should win.
Height alone tells us nothing. Next time, count the green leaves and check that each stem stands up by themself.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a reason from the light test. Then say one thing that another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses evidence: the dark seedlings in the light test were tallest but pale and weak, just like Zoya's. It also gives the others their due. Rukmini Mami is right that changing a rule at the end is unfair to everyone who followed it. Kavitha's idea fixes the problem for next year.
items.why: There is a real trade-off here. A rule everyone agreed to matters. But the rule measured the wrong thing, because height alone does not show health.
items.context: This question is about the story A Stripe of Sun. In a building in Chennai, children had a contest to grow the tallest moong. Zoya's moong, in a dim window facing a wall, grew tallest but was pale and fell over. Arjun's moong, on the sunny terrace, was short and dark green.

items.p: Anand's money plant sits in a dark corner of the hall. The plant grows long, thin stems with small leaves far apart. Which need is in short supply? What would you change?
items.a: Light is in short supply. The plant is stretching towards light, like the dark seedlings. I would move the plant near a bright window, or bounce light onto them with a mirror or a steel plate, like Zoya's thali.
items.why: Long, thin stems with leaves far apart are the clue of too little light. A strong answer names the need and gives a cure that adds light.

items.p: Moong sprouts kept in a fridge for 3 days are dead and will never grow again.
items.why: False. Cold slows the sprouts down, but 3 days in a fridge does not kill them. Back in a warm room they start growing again. 'Not growing' is not the same as 'dead'.
items.context: This question is about the warmth test. Moong sprouts are kept in the dark in a fridge, a room cupboard and a warm spot, and measured each day.

chart.title: The warmth test: total growth of 5 sprouts in 3 days (made-up results)

items.p: A pale yellow seedling from the dark turns green within a day or two after being put in the light.
items.why: True. In the light, the seedling starts making green chlorophyll. They only die if they stay in the dark until their stored food runs out.
items.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.

items.p: Growing plants with their roots in water mixed with minerals, and no soil, is called ____.
items.why: Hydroponic farms grow lettuce and herbs this way, on rooftops and even in space.

items.p: Put the steps of the light test in order.
items: Sow 5 moong in each of 6 cups
Cover 3 cups with a box
Water every cup the same amount every morning
Measure the tallest seedling in each cup
Draw a bar chart and write a conclusion
items.a: order shown
items.why: First you set up the cups. Then you change the one thing. Then you care for them all the same way, and measure. Last, you show and explain your results.
items.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.

items.p: A girl goes away for 10 days in May. She stands her tulsi pot in a bucket full of water, so the soil will not dry out. Predict what she finds when she comes back. What would work better?
items.a: The soil will be soaked for 10 days, so the roots get no air. The tulsi will probably have yellow leaves and rotting roots, like the SOAKED cups. A better idea is a slow drip: a bottle with a tiny hole in the cap, upside down in the soil, or a wet cotton string from a jar of water into the pot.
items.why: A strong answer uses the water test to predict, and gives a way to give a little water at a time.

worksheets.title: Just Right, Deep Down and in Space (challenge)

items.p: In the warmth test, the warm spot at 33 °C gave the most growth. Can you say that moong grows best in the hottest place possible?
opts: Yes, the hotter the better
Yes, because the warm bar was the tallest
No. We only tested three temperatures, and above a certain point heat harms plants
items.why: We did not test hotter places, so we cannot say what happens there. Other experiments show that great heat harms plants. Good scientists claim only what their test showed.
items.context: This question is about the warmth test. Moong sprouts are kept in the dark in a fridge, a room cupboard and a warm spot, and measured each day.

chart.title: The warmth test: total growth of 5 sprouts in 3 days (made-up results)

items.p: Under green see-through cellophane, seedlings often grow taller and paler, as if they were in dim light. Why?
opts: Green is a cold colour
Leaves use red and blue light most, and bounce back much of the green, so they get little of the light they use
Green cellophane is poisonous
items.why: A leaf looks green because it reflects more green light than other colours. So green is the colour a leaf uses least. Picking 'cold colour' mixes up how colours feel to us with what plants use.
items.context: This question is about the coloured light test. Four cups of seedlings are covered with clear, red, blue or green see-through cellophane for a week.

items.p: A plant stands in a dark corner. A girl gives the plant extra fertiliser, but they grow no better. What does this show?
opts: Light was the need in shortest supply, so more minerals could not help
Fertiliser never works
The plant was dead
items.why: This is the idea of the shortest plank. Extra of one need does not help if another need is in short supply. Picking 'fertiliser never works' stretches one result to every case.

items.p: Long ago, two scientists asked what a plant's body is made from.

views.who: Jan Baptist van Helmont, in what is now Belgium, 1600s
views.says: I grew a willow tree in a pot for five years and gave the tree only rainwater. The tree gained about 74 kilograms, but the soil lost only about 57 grams. So a plant is made from water.
I grew mint in jars of rainwater, river water and muddy water. The mint in the muddiest water grew most. So plants need something from the soil, not only water.

items.ask: Whose evidence convinces you more? Explain why. Then say what the other scientist got right, and what both of them missed.
items.a: A strong answer weighs the evidence. Van Helmont's numbers are striking: the soil hardly changed, so the tree's weight cannot have come from the soil. Woodward's test is fairer, because he compared different waters side by side. Both were partly right. Plants take in a lot of water, and they need minerals from the soil. But both missed the air: most of a plant's dry body is built from a gas in the air, using light.
items.why: Each scientist had real evidence. Van Helmont was right that the soil gives very little weight. Woodward was right that the soil gives something plants need. Neither of them knew that plants build their bodies mostly from the air.

items.p: In the light test, what shows that seedlings can sense light, even though they have no eyes?
opts: The seedlings in the dark were wetter
Nothing shows it
The seedlings in the dark grew in a different way: tall, pale, with folded leaves
items.why: The dark seedlings changed how they grew, so they must have sensed the dark. Plants sense light with special molecules called photoreceptors, which change when light falls on them.
items.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.

items.p: Scientists have found that phytochrome B, a light-sensing molecule in plants, also changes faster when it is warm.
items.why: True. In 2016, two teams of scientists found that phytochrome B also works like a thermometer. Plants seem to have other warmth sensors too, and scientists are still working out how they all fit together.

items.p: In January 2019, cotton seeds sprouted on the far side of the Moon, inside a sealed can on the Chinese spacecraft Chang'e 4. Why did the experiment end after only a few days?
opts: The cotton was eaten
The long, freezing Moon night came, and it got far too cold
There was too much water
items.why: A night on the Moon lasts about two Earth weeks and is extremely cold. Warmth is one of a plant's needs. Picking 'too much water' misses that the big problem on the Moon is the cold.
items.context: Chang'e 4 is a Chinese spacecraft that landed on the far side of the Moon in January 2019. It carried a small sealed can with seeds, soil, water and air.

items.p: Why does warmth make a sprout grow faster?
opts: Warm molecules move faster and bump into each other more often, so the work of growing goes faster
Heat is a kind of food for the sprout
Warmth makes the sprout lighter
items.why: Temperature tells how fast molecules are moving. Faster molecules meet more often, so the plant's helper molecules, called enzymes, work faster. Picking 'heat is food' mixes up warmth with food. The sprout's food is stored in the seed.

items.p: A plant in a pot on a hot, sunny terrace can droop at midday, even when their soil is still damp.
items.why: True. On a hot afternoon, leaves lose water into the air faster than the roots can drink it. The plant droops, then stands up again in the cool evening. Check the soil before watering: damp soil means wait, not pour.

items.p: More is not always better. Match each 'too much' to what it does to a plant.
pairs: the roots get no air and start to rot
the plant loses water fast and their enzymes stop working
the salty soil draws water out of the roots
the plant grows tall, pale and weak
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Every need has a just-right amount. Too little and too much can both harm a plant.

items.p: Ishita, a girl in Class 4, says: 'If a little fertiliser is good for my plant, a lot must be even better.' What would you tell her? How could she test her idea fairly?
items.a: More is not always better. Too much fertiliser makes the soil salty, and that can damage roots. To test it, she could grow 3 cups with no fertiliser, 3 with a little and 3 with a lot. Everything else stays the same: seeds, soil, light and water. Then she measures and compares after two weeks.
items.why: A strong answer challenges the 'more is better' idea and plans a test with three amounts, like the water test.

items.p: Bose's growth magnifier makes a plant's growth look 4 times bigger. The pointer moved 20 millimetres in 10 hours. How much did the plant really grow in those 10 hours? How much is that in one hour?
items.a: 20 divided by 4 is 5. So the plant grew 5 millimetres in 10 hours. 5 millimetres shared between 10 hours is half a millimetre each hour.
items.why: Divide the pointer's movement by how much the lever magnifies. Then share it between the hours.
items.context: In the growth magnifier activity, a straw lever is tied to the top of a growing plant. The long end of the straw moves 4 times as far as the plant grows.

items.p: In the light test, we kept some seedlings in the dark until they were weak. Was that fair to the seedlings? Give one reason for and one reason against.
items.a: For: we learnt something important about what plants need, and we put the dark seedlings back in the light at the end, so most of them turned green. Against: we made living beings struggle on purpose. Any answer with a real reason on each side is good.
items.why: There is no single right answer. The point is to weigh both sides.

items.p: Astronauts plan to grow food on the Moon. List what the plants will need, and say where the astronauts could get each one.
items.a: Light: from the Sun during the long Moon day, or from lamps. Water: brought from Earth, or made from ice near the Moon's poles. Air: made and pumped into a sealed greenhouse. Warmth: heaters and covers, because Moon nights are freezing. Minerals: from Moon soil, with extra added.
items.why: A strong answer covers every need from this unit, and notices that Earth gives most of them for free.

items.p: A fern on a sunny terrace has brown, crispy edges. A cactus in a dark bathroom is pale and leaning. What is wrong with each plant? What would you do?
items.a: The fern is getting too much sun and heat. Move the fern to a shady, cooler place and keep their soil damp. The cactus is getting too little light. Move the cactus to a sunny window, and water them only a little.
items.why: Each kind of plant has their own just right. The same place can be too much for one plant and too little for another.

items.p: Draw the shortest-plank bucket for Zoya's moong in the dim window. Label each plank with a need. Make the shortest plank the need that held the moong back.
items.a: A bucket with planks for light, water, air, warmth and minerals. The light plank is the shortest, and water spills out over it.
items.why: Zoya's moong had water, air, warmth and soil, but very little light. So light was their shortest plank.
items.art: An outline of a wooden bucket with five empty planks to label.
