experiments.title: The Light Test: what happens in the dark?
experiments.question: Do moong seedlings need light to grow well? What happens to them in the dark?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After a week, will the seedlings in the dark be taller or shorter than the ones in the light? Will they be green or another colour? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the light. Use 6 cups that are the same, the same soil, and 5 moong seeds in each cup. Put all 6 cups side by side near the same bright window, out of strong afternoon sun, so the box does not get hotter than the open cups. Cover 3 of them with a cardboard box. Water every cup with the same tablespoon of water each morning. Measure every cup at the same time of day. We use 3 cups for each, because one cup could be a fluke.

Open green leaves on the tallest seedling

materials.item: 6 small plastic or paper cups, such as yoghurt cups, each with a small hole poked in the bottom
potting soil from a nursery, or soil from a pot at home. No soil? Fold wet tissue into each cup instead, because moong can grow for a week on the food in the seed.
30 moong seeds, soaked in water overnight
a cardboard box big enough to cover 3 cups and keep out all light
a tray or old plate to stand the cups on
a tablespoon for watering
a 30 cm ruler
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up pokes the holes in the cups. Wash hands after touching soil. Do not eat the seeds.

schedule.what: Sow 5 soaked moong in each of 6 cups. Write your prediction. Put 3 cups under the box and 3 beside it in the light.
Water every cup with 1 tablespoon. Put the box back quickly. Do this every morning until Day 7.
Water, then measure the tallest seedling in each cup. Write the heights and colours.
Water every cup the same.
Water and measure again.
Water every cup the same.
Measure, count the open green leaves on the tallest seedling in each cup, compare and draw a bar chart. Say what you think, what you saw and why.
Put the dark cups in the light. Look again tomorrow. Do they turn green?

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw two bar charts: one of the heights on Day 7, and one of the number of open green leaves.

flow.do: 1. Put the soaked moong in a bowl. 2. Ask your child to predict what will happen in the dark, and write it down.
flow.say: Some seedlings will grow in the light, and some in the dark. In a week, which do you think will be taller? Which will be greener?
flow.kid: Some moong will grow in the light. Some will grow in the dark. Guess: which will be taller? Which will be greener? Write it down.

ask.q: Why do you think that?
good: Plants need light, so the dark ones will be small.
They might grow up to look for light.

flow.parent: Most children predict the dark seedlings will be smaller. That is a fine prediction. The surprise is part of the lesson.
flow.context: This is the first step of the light test. You grow moong seedlings in the light and in the dark, and keep everything else the same.

flow.do: 1. Fill 6 cups with soil to about one finger-width below the rim. 2. Press 5 soaked moong into each cup, about as deep as your fingernail. 3. Water each cup with 1 tablespoon. 4. Label 3 cups LIGHT and 3 cups DARK. 5. Stand all 6 on a tray near a bright window, out of strong afternoon sun. 6. Cover the 3 DARK cups with the box.
flow.say: We'll keep everything the same except one thing. Same cups, same soil, same seeds, same water, same window. The only difference is the box.
flow.kid: Fill 6 cups with soil. Push 5 moong into each one. Give each cup 1 spoon of water. Put a box over 3 cups. Everything else stays the same.

ask.q: What is the one thing we are changing?
good: Whether the cup is under the box.

ask.q: What are we keeping the same?
good: The soil, the seeds, the cups, the water, the window.

flow.parent: Moong usually comes up in 2 or 3 days in a warm room. In a cold winter room it can take 5 days or more, so add those days to the plan. If nothing has come up by Day 6, sow again in a warmer place.

flow.do: Every morning, lift the box for as short a time as you can. Water every cup with the same tablespoon of water. Put the box back straight away.
flow.say: We lift the box quickly, so the dark cups get as little light as possible. And every cup gets exactly the same water.
flow.kid: Lift the box. Give every cup 1 spoon of water. Put the box back fast. The dark cups must stay dark.
flow.wait: Water every morning. Measure on Day 3 and Day 5.

flow.do: On Day 3 and Day 5: 1. Find the tallest seedling in each cup. 2. Stand the ruler on the soil beside them, with the 0 at the soil. 3. Read the number at the highest point of the seedling. 4. Write the height and the colour in the table.
flow.say: Put the zero of the ruler right at the soil. Read the number at the very top of the tallest seedling.
flow.kid: Stand the ruler on the soil. Zero goes at the bottom. Read the number at the top of the tallest seedling. Write it down.
flow.parent: Dark seedlings often grow with a hooked top. Measure to the highest point, not along the bend. If your child finds it hard to read the small marks, round to the nearest centimetre for now.

check.q: Where should the 0 on the ruler go when you measure a seedling?
options: At the top of the cup
At the end of the ruler, wherever it is
check.why: The height of a plant is measured from the soil to the top. So the 0 goes at the soil. Picking 'the top of the cup' is a common slip. Then the part of the stem inside the cup is not counted.

flow.do: On Day 7: 1. Take the box off. 2. Line up all 6 cups. 3. Measure the tallest seedling in each cup. 4. Count the open green leaves on that tallest seedling. 5. Look closely at the stems and colours.
flow.say: Let's look at all of them together. Which are taller? Which are greener? Which are stronger?
flow.kid: Take the box off. Line up all the cups. Measure the tallest seedling in each. Count their open green leaves. What do you notice?

ask.q: What do the dark seedlings look like?
good: Their leaves are tiny and closed.

ask.q: Was your prediction right?

flow.parent: Usually the dark seedlings are taller, but yellow or white, thin and floppy, with small folded leaves. The light seedlings are shorter, thicker and green, with open leaves. This surprises most children.

check.q: The dark seedlings grew taller than the light seedlings. Does that mean they are healthier?
options: No. They are tall because they are stretching to find light, and they are pale and weak
check.why: In the dark, a seedling uses their stored food to grow tall and thin, looking for light. They cannot make green chlorophyll or new food. So they are weak and will die when their stored food runs out. Picking 'taller means healthier' is the most common idea. That is why we also count the green leaves.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table on Day 7
cols: Open green leaves on the tallest seedling

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the Day 7 heights. Use the middle height of the 3 LIGHT cups and of the 3 DARK cups.
flow.say: To find the middle height, put the 3 numbers in order and take the middle one. Then draw one bar for LIGHT and one for DARK.
flow.kid: Put the 3 LIGHT heights in order. The middle one is your LIGHT bar. Do the same for DARK. Draw both bars.
flow.parent: With the made-up numbers, LIGHT is 8, 8, 9, so the middle is 8. DARK is 13, 14, 15, so the middle is 14. Using the middle value stops one odd cup from fooling us.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. First, what you think now. Second, what you saw. Third, why you think it happened.

What I saw: the dark seedlings were 14 cm tall but yellow and floppy, with no open green leaves. The light ones were 8 cm, green and strong. Why: without light they could not make food or green colour. So they used their stored food to stretch up and look for light.

flow.do: On Day 8, move the dark cups into the light. Look again the next day.
flow.say: Let's give the dark seedlings their light back. What do you think will happen by tomorrow?
flow.kid: Put the dark cups in the light. Look tomorrow. Do they turn green?
flow.parent: Within a day, the yellow seedlings usually start to turn green, because they make chlorophyll once they have light. Very weak seedlings that have fallen over may not recover. Giving the light back is a kind way to end the test, too.
flow.think: The dark seedlings had no eyes. How did they know they were in the dark?

experiments.title: The Water Test: too little, just right, too much
experiments.question: How much water do moong seedlings need? Is more water always better?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which cups will do best: no water, just right water, or soaked all the time? Which will do worst? Write your guesses and reasons.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the water. Grow all 9 cups of seedlings the same way for 5 days first. Then give 3 cups no water, and 3 cups 1 tablespoon every morning. Stand the last 3 cups in a deep dish of water that always comes up to the level of the soil inside the cups, so the soil stays soaked to the top. Keep the cups side by side on the same windowsill. Measure every cup at the same time of day.
results_table: Leaves: firm, drooping, yellow or dry?

materials.item: 9 small plastic cups or yoghurt cups, each with a small hole poked in the bottom. Paper cups go soft standing in water.
potting soil from a nursery, or soil from a pot at home
45 moong seeds, soaked overnight
2 trays or old plates, and 1 deep dish or a cut-off plastic bottle bottom
a tablespoon for watering
a 30 cm ruler
labels: NONE, JUST RIGHT, SOAKED

experiments.safety: A grown-up pokes the holes in the cups. Wash hands after touching soil. Tip out the SOAKED dish and fill it with fresh water every second day, so mosquitoes cannot breed in it. Throw away soggy, smelly soil outside or in the dustbin, not in the kitchen sink.

schedule.what: Sow 5 soaked moong in each of 9 cups. Water every cup with 1 tablespoon and put them all on the windowsill.
Water all 9 cups the same. Do this every morning until Day 5.
Measure all cups. Write your predictions. Start the three treatments: none, just right, soaked.
Water the JUST RIGHT cups. Tip out the SOAKED dish and fill it with fresh water. Write one line about each group.
Water, change the dish water and measure.
Water, change the dish water and look closely at the leaves.
Final measuring. Tip one cup from each group out to look at the roots. Draw a bar chart and say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar chart of the middle height of each group on Day 14. Draw what the roots looked like in each group.

flow.do: 1. Fill 9 cups with soil. 2. Press 5 soaked moong into each. 3. Water each cup with 1 tablespoon. 4. Put all 9 on a tray on a bright windowsill.
flow.say: First we grow all 9 cups exactly the same way, so they start the test the same.
flow.kid: Fill 9 cups with soil. Push 5 moong into each. Give each 1 spoon of water. Put them all on the windowsill.
flow.wait: Let the seedlings grow for 5 days. Water all 9 cups the same, 1 tablespoon every morning.
flow.context: This is the first step of the water test. You grow 9 cups of moong seedlings, then give some no water, some just the right amount and some far too much.

flow.do: On Day 6: 1. Measure the tallest seedling in each cup and write it down. 2. Label 3 cups NONE, 3 JUST RIGHT and 3 SOAKED. 3. Stand the 3 SOAKED cups in a deep dish. Fill the dish with water up to the soil inside the cups. 4. Put all the cups back side by side.
flow.say: Now the test begins. These get no water at all. These get 1 spoon every morning. And these stand in water all the time. Which do you think will do best?
flow.kid: Measure every cup. Put labels on: NONE, JUST RIGHT, SOAKED. Stand the SOAKED cups in a dish of water. Which will do best? Guess.

ask.q: Which do you think will do best? Why?
good: Just right, because too much is bad too.

flow.parent: Many children predict the soaked cups will do best. Let them. The test will answer it.

flow.do: 1. Every morning, water the JUST RIGHT cups with 1 tablespoon. 2. Give the NONE cups nothing. 3. Every second day, tip out the SOAKED dish. Fill it again with fresh water, up to the soil inside the cups. 4. Press a finger into the soil of one cup from each group and write: dry, damp or soggy.
flow.say: Feel the soil. Dry, damp or soggy? Write it down for each group.
flow.kid: Water only the JUST RIGHT cups. Change the dish water every second day. Feel the soil. Dry, damp or soggy?
flow.parent: Changing the dish water matters. Mosquitoes need several days in still water to grow from eggs, so fresh water every second day stops them.

flow.do: On Day 8 or 10, look closely at the leaves in each group together.
flow.say: Let's be plant doctors. What do the leaves look like in each group?
flow.kid: Look at the leaves in each group. Are they firm, drooping, yellow or dry?

check.q: The NONE cups have drooping, floppy leaves. What is the plant telling us?
check.why: A plant that droops in dry soil is wilting. Their cells are going soft because there is not enough water to fill them. Picking 'light' is a sensible guess, because plants in the dark also flop. But in the dark they are pale and tall. These are green and drooping, and their soil is dry.

flow.do: On Day 14: 1. Measure the tallest seedling in each cup. 2. Gently tip one cup from each group onto newspaper. 3. Wash the soil off the roots in a bowl of water. 4. Compare the roots.
flow.say: Let's look at the hidden part, the roots. What do the roots look like in each group?
flow.kid: Measure every cup. Then tip out one cup from each group. Wash the roots gently. Compare them.

ask.q: What do the SOAKED roots look like?
What do the JUST RIGHT roots look like?

flow.parent: Usually the NONE seedlings droop within 2 or 3 days, then dry up and turn brown, with thin dry roots. JUST RIGHT seedlings are green and firm, with white, spreading roots. SOAKED seedlings are often yellowing and shorter, with brown, soft roots. In some weather the soaked cups survive for longer. That is real science too. Write down what you actually saw.

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the middle height in each group on Day 14.
flow.say: One bar for each group. Put the three heights in order and use the middle one.
flow.kid: Draw a bar for NONE, JUST RIGHT and SOAKED. Use the middle height of each group.

flow.kid: Say or write three things. First, what you think now. Second, what you saw. Third, why you think it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: moong needs some water, but not too much. What I saw: the JUST RIGHT seedlings were 13 cm and green. The NONE ones dried up, and the SOAKED ones were 8 cm and yellow with brown roots. Why: without water the cells go soft. In soaked soil the roots cannot get air, so they rot.
flow.think: Rice grows standing in water. Why don't the rice plants drown like our moong? (Hint: rice has air channels that carry air down to their roots.)

experiments.title: The Warmth Test: cold, cool or warm?
experiments.question: Do moong sprouts grow faster when they are warm or when they are cold?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Some sprouts go in the fridge, some in a room cupboard and some in a warm spot. After 3 days, which will have grown longest? Write your guess and reason.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the warmth. Use 3 steel katoris or bowls that are the same, each with the same folded wet cloth and 10 sprouts. The fridge is dark inside, so cover all 3 bowls with a plate to make them all dark. Put the same amount of water in each. Measure all three at the same time each day.

materials.item: about 40 moong seeds, soaked overnight and then kept in a closed box on a wet cloth for 1 day, until tiny roots show. In a cold room this can take 2 days.
3 steel katoris or small bowls of the same size, and 3 plates to cover them
a clean cotton cloth or paper napkin, folded to fit each bowl
a teaspoon
a room thermometer, if you have one
a 30 cm ruler

experiments.safety: For the warm spot, use a closed cupboard in the warmest room, or the top of the fridge near the back, where warm air comes out. Never use the stove, the oven, a heater or a flame. Do not eat the sprouts afterwards.

schedule.what: Set up the three bowls. Measure the sprouts. Put one bowl in the fridge, one in a room cupboard and one in a warm spot.
Measure the 5 longest sprouts in each bowl. Read the temperature in each place.
Measure again.
Final measuring. Work out how much each bowl grew. Draw a bar chart. Move the fridge bowl into the room and watch.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. For each place, take the first total away from the last total. Draw one bar for each place.

flow.do: Show your child the sprouted moong and ask for a prediction.
flow.say: We'll keep some sprouts cold, some cool and some warm. Which do you think will grow the most in 3 days?
flow.kid: Some sprouts go in the fridge. Some go in a cupboard. Some go somewhere warm. Guess: which will grow most?
flow.context: This is the first step of the warmth test. You keep moong sprouts in a cold, a cool and a warm place, in the dark, and measure how much they grow.

flow.do: 1. Fold a wet cloth flat in each bowl. 2. Wet each with exactly 4 teaspoons of water. 3. Put 10 sprouts on the cloth in each bowl. 4. Measure the 5 longest sprouts in each bowl, from the tip of the root to the top, and add them up. 5. Cover each bowl with a plate.
flow.say: The fridge is dark inside. So we cover all three bowls with a plate, to make them all dark. That way only the warmth is different.
flow.kid: Put a folded wet cloth in 3 bowls. Add 4 spoons of water to each. Put 10 sprouts in each. Measure 5 sprouts. Cover each bowl with a plate.

ask.q: Why do we cover all three bowls, not just the fridge one?
good: So only the warmth is different.

flow.parent: Adding up 5 sprouts gives one number for each bowl, and evens out small and big sprouts. Sprouts of 1 cm, 2 cm, 1 cm, 1 cm and 1 cm add up to 6 cm. Lift each sprout gently, because their root may stick to the cloth.

flow.do: 1. Put one bowl in the fridge, not the freezer. 2. Put one bowl in a cupboard in a room. 3. Put one bowl in a warm spot, like a cupboard in the warmest room or the top of the fridge. 4. If you have a thermometer, leave it in each place for 5 minutes and read it.
flow.say: Let's read the temperature in each place. The fridge is about 5 degrees. A room in India is often between 20 and 32 degrees.
flow.kid: Put one bowl in the fridge. Put one in a cupboard. Put one somewhere warm. Read the thermometer in each place.
flow.parent: Never use the stove, oven, a heater or a flame for the warm spot. If your warm spot turns out no warmer than the cupboard, the test still works with two places: the fridge and the cupboard. In winter, a warm spot makes a bigger difference.

flow.do: On Day 2 and Day 3: take each bowl out, measure the 5 longest sprouts and add them up. Add 1 teaspoon of water if the cloth is drying. Put each bowl back quickly.
flow.say: Measure the 5 longest sprouts and add them up. Which bowl is growing fastest?
flow.kid: Measure the 5 longest sprouts in each bowl. Add them up. Write the total. Put the bowl back fast.

check.q: You add water to the warm bowl because its cloth is drying. What should you do for the other two bowls?
options: Add the same amount, so the water stays the same in all three
check.why: In a fair test, only the warmth should be different. If one bowl gets more water, water changes too. Picking 'nothing' usually means thinking only about the bowl in front of you, and not about keeping the test fair.

flow.do: On Day 4: 1. Measure one last time. 2. For each bowl, take the Day 1 total away from the last total. That is how much they grew. 3. Draw a bar for each place.
flow.say: Take the first total away from the last total. That tells us how much each bowl grew. Let's draw one bar for each.
flow.kid: Take the first number away from the last number. That is how much they grew. Draw one bar for each place.

flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. First, what you think now. Second, what you saw. Third, why you think it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: moong sprouts grow faster when they are warm. What I saw: in 3 days the fridge sprouts grew 1 cm. The cupboard ones grew 18 cm and the warm ones 24 cm. Why: warmth makes the tiny helpers inside the sprouts work faster.

flow.do: Move the fridge bowl into the room cupboard. Look again in 2 days.
flow.say: Are the fridge sprouts dead, or only waiting? Let's warm them up and see.
flow.kid: Put the fridge bowl in the cupboard. Look in 2 days. Are the sprouts dead, or only waiting?
flow.parent: The cold sprouts usually start growing again in the warmth. Cold slowed them down. A few may have been harmed, because moong comes from warm places and does not like long cold.
flow.think: Our warm spot was best. Would an even hotter place, like a terrace at 46 degrees, be even better? Why not?

experiments.context: This is the warmth test. You put moong sprouts in a fridge, a room cupboard and a warm spot, all in the dark. You measure how much they grow in 3 days.

experiments.title: Coloured Light: does the colour matter?
experiments.question: Do seedlings grow differently under red, blue, green or clear see-through covers?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which colour of light will grow the greenest, strongest seedlings? Which will grow the weakest? Plants are green. Do you think they like green light best? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Change only the colour of the cover. Use 4 cups of seedlings sown on the same day, the same soil and the same water. Make 4 cone-shaped covers of the same size, from clear, red, blue and green cellophane. Stand the cups side by side in the same bright place.

materials.item: 4 cups of moong seedlings about 2 cm tall. Sow 5 soaked moong in each cup 3 or 4 days before, and keep them on the windowsill.
cellophane sheets: clear, red, blue and green
sticky tape and 4 thin sticks or straws to hold the covers up
a 30 cm ruler

experiments.safety: Leave a small gap at the bottom of each cover so air can get in. Do not leave the cups in hot afternoon sun, because the covers can trap heat.

schedule.what: Make 4 cellophane covers and put one over each cup. Write your predictions.
Water every cup the same each morning, and look through the covers.
Take off the covers. Measure, compare colour and leaves, and say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw each seedling in their colour of light.

flow.do: 1. Push 4 sticks or straws into the soil around each cup's edge. 2. Roll a sheet of cellophane into a tall cone or tube and tape it to the sticks. 3. Leave a small gap at the bottom for air. 4. Use one colour for each cup: clear, red, blue, green.
flow.say: Each cup gets a coloured window. The clear one lets all the colours of sunlight through. The others let mostly one colour through.
flow.kid: Make a tall see-through hat for each cup. One clear, one red, one blue, one green. Leave a gap at the bottom for air.
flow.context: This is the first step of the coloured light test. You cover cups of seedlings with clear, red, blue and green see-through sheets and see how they grow.

ask.q: Plants are green. Which colour do you think they like best?
good: Maybe not green. Maybe they bounce green light away.

flow.do: Every morning, lift each cover for a moment, water each cup with the same 1 tablespoon and put the cover back.
flow.say: Same water for every cup. Only the colour is different.
flow.kid: Lift each hat. Give each cup 1 spoon of water. Put the hat back.
flow.wait: Water every morning. Look on Day 7.

flow.do: On Day 7: 1. Take off the covers. 2. Measure the tallest seedling in each cup. 3. Compare leaf colour, stem thickness and how much each seedling leans.
flow.say: Which seedlings look most like the ones in full light? Which look most like the ones in the dark?
flow.kid: Take off the hats. Measure each cup. Which seedlings are greenest and strongest? Which look like they were in the dark?
flow.parent: Clear usually gives the sturdiest green seedlings. Under red they are often a little taller and thinner. Blue usually gives short, green seedlings. Green often looks most like the dark cups, taller and paler. Results at home vary. Cellophane sheets also let different amounts of light through, so this test is not perfectly fair. That is worth talking about.

check.q: Plants are green because their leaves bounce back much of the green light. So, under green cellophane, what do the seedlings mostly get?
options: The light they use least, so they grow as if in dim light
check.why: A leaf looks green because it uses red and blue light most and bounces back more green light. Under green cellophane, the seedlings get mostly the colour they use least. So they often stretch and stay pale, as in dim light. Picking 'the light they use best' is a very common guess, because plants are green.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why. Then talk about what made the test less than perfectly fair.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see? Why? And was our test perfectly fair?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. First, what you think now. Second, what you saw. Third, why you think it happened. Then think: was the test perfectly fair?
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: plants use some colours of light better than others. What I saw: under green, the seedlings were taller and paler than under clear or red. Why: plants bounce back green light, so they get less of the light they use. The test was not perfectly fair, because the coloured sheets let different amounts of light through.
flow.think: Astronauts grow lettuce under red and blue lamps, which make a pink glow. Why not plain green lamps?

experiments.context: This is the coloured light test. You cover 4 cups of seedlings with clear, red, blue and green see-through sheets, and compare how they grow after a week.

activities.title: Pale Sprouts

materials.item: a handful of moong, soaked in water overnight
a steel tiffin or any box with a lid, and a wet cloth
a plate and a second wet cloth
a potato or onion with shoots from a dark basket, if you have one

activities.safety: Wash hands after handling the sprouts. Do not eat sprouts that have stood on the windowsill for days.

schedule.what: Soak a handful of moong in water overnight. Next morning, drain it and close it in a tiffin on a wet cloth.
Open the tiffin. Notice the colour of the shoots. Put half the sprouts on the windowsill and close the rest back in the tiffin.
Compare a windowsill sprout with a tiffin sprout.

activities.record: Draw a sprout from the tiffin and a sprout from the windowsill. Write three things you notice and one thing you wonder.

flow.do: 1. Soak a handful of moong in a bowl of water overnight. 2. Next morning, drain it. 3. Spread it on a wet cloth in a steel tiffin and close the lid.
flow.say: We are going to grow some sprouts in a closed box. In two days we will open it and look.
flow.kid: Soak some moong overnight. Then put it on a wet cloth in a tiffin. Close the lid.
flow.wait: Leave the tiffin closed for 1 or 2 days, until the shoots are as long as a fingernail.
flow.parent: In a warm room the shoots grow in a day. In a cold winter room it can take 2 or 3 days. Sprinkle a little water on the cloth if it dries.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pale Sprouts. It is a way into the unit: something real to notice before any explaining.

flow.do: 1. Open the tiffin together. 2. Look closely at the shoots and their colour. 3. If you have a potato or onion with shoots from a dark basket, look at that too.
flow.say: Look at these shoots. What do you notice about their colour? Don't explain yet. Just notice.
flow.kid: Open the tiffin. Look at the shoots. What colour are they? What do you notice?

ask.q: What do you notice?
What do you wonder?

flow.parent: Do not explain yet. The light test will answer the question. Write down your child's wonderings, so you can come back to them. If you have a garden or a park nearby, also lift a brick or flowerpot that has lain on grass for a week. The grass underneath is pale for the same reason.

flow.do: 1. Put half the sprouts on a wet cloth on a plate, on a bright windowsill. 2. Put the other half back in the tiffin and close it. 3. Sprinkle both lots with the same amount of water.
flow.say: Let's do a small test. Half go in the light, and half stay in the dark. What do you think will happen by tomorrow? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put half the sprouts on the windowsill. Close the rest in the tiffin. What will happen by tomorrow? Why?

ask.q: What do you predict? Why?
good: The ones in the light will go green, because leaves are green in the light.
Nothing will change, because sprouts are always white.

flow.do: The next day, put a windowsill sprout and a tiffin sprout side by side on white paper. Compare their colour, especially near the top.
flow.say: Which one is greener? What was the only thing that was different between them?
flow.kid: Put one sprout from each place on white paper. Which is greener? What was different?
flow.parent: Many windowsill sprouts show a green tinge near the top, and their seed halves look greener. The tiffin sprouts stay pale. If the change is faint, leave them one more day. Both lots got water and air. Only the light was different.

check.q: Both lots of sprouts had water and air. What did the windowsill sprouts get that the tiffin sprouts did not?
check.why: The closed tiffin kept out the light. Without light, a sprout does not make their green chlorophyll, so they stay pale. Picking 'water' or 'air' is a sensible guess. But both lots got the same water, and the tiffin had air inside.

flow.think: If the tiffin sprouts stayed in the dark for a week, what do you think would happen to them?

activities.context: This is a short noticing activity to start the unit. You grow moong sprouts in a closed tiffin, look at their pale shoots, and then put half of them in the light.

activities.title: Measure Like a Scientist: the paper-strip growth chart

materials.item: a 30 cm ruler with millimetre marks
a growing plant, such as a seedling from the light test or a bean plant
a long strip of paper about 2 cm wide, scissors and glue
a big sheet of paper or a notebook page

schedule.what: Practise measuring things in centimetres and millimetres. Measure the plant and cut and stick the first strip.
Measure, cut a strip and stick it next to yesterday's.
After 10 days of strips, look at the chart. Which day did they grow most?

activities.record: A row of paper strips, one for each day, each as long as the plant was tall that day. Write the date and the height under each strip.

flow.do: 1. Look at the ruler together: find 0, the big numbered centimetre lines and the tiny millimetre lines. 2. Measure 4 things: a fingernail, a pencil, a matchbox and a leaf.
flow.say: The big numbers are centimetres. Between each number there are 10 tiny marks. Each tiny mark is a millimetre. Ten millimetres make one centimetre.
flow.kid: Find the 0 on your ruler. Find the big numbers. They are centimetres. Count the tiny marks between 1 and 2. There are 10. Each is a millimetre.

ask.q: Your pencil reaches 2 tiny marks past the 14. How long is it?

flow.parent: Many children start measuring from the end of the ruler, not the 0. Show that some rulers have a gap before the 0.
flow.context: This is the first step of the paper-strip growth chart. You learn to measure carefully with a ruler, then make a chart of a plant's growth out of paper strips.

check.q: A leaf starts at the 0 and ends exactly on the 6. How long is it?
check.why: The big numbered lines are centimetres. So a leaf that ends at the 6 is 6 centimetres long. That is the same as 60 millimetres. Picking '6 millimetres' usually means mixing up the big lines and the tiny marks.

flow.do: 1. Measure the plant from the soil to the top. 2. Cut a paper strip exactly as long as the plant. 3. Stick it at the left of the big sheet, standing up, with its bottom on a line. 4. Write the date and height under it.
flow.say: This strip is exactly as tall as our plant today. Tomorrow we'll cut another one.
flow.kid: Measure your plant. Cut a paper strip just as long. Stick it on the big sheet. Write the date and the number under it.

flow.do: Each day at the same time, measure again, cut a new strip and stick it beside the last one.
flow.say: Same time every day, so it's fair.
flow.kid: Same time every day. Measure. Cut a strip. Stick it next to yesterday's.

flow.do: After 10 strips, look at the chart together. Find the day they grew most, by finding the biggest jump between two strips.
flow.say: Our strips have made a chart. Look for the biggest jump from one strip to the next. That was the day they grew most.
flow.kid: Look at your strips. They make a chart! Find the biggest jump. That day, your plant grew most.

ask.q: How much did they grow on their best day?
good: I took the height on the day before away from the height on that day. For example, 15 millimetres.

ask.q: Did they grow the same amount every day?
good: No, some days more, some days less.

flow.parent: This paper chart is a real bar chart. Each strip is a bar. Children who make one usually understand bar charts straight away.
flow.think: Was the weather different on the day they grew most? Warmer? Sunnier?

activities.context: This activity teaches careful measuring with a ruler. Then you cut a paper strip as tall as your plant every day. Stuck side by side, the strips make a growth chart.

activities.title: Plant Doctor: which need is missing?

materials.item: 5 or more plants at home, on the balcony, in your building or at a neighbour's. If you can find only one or two, also examine the moong cups from the light and water tests
a notebook and pencil
a magnifying glass, if you have one

activities.safety: Ask the owner before touching anyone else's plant. Wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Examine 5 plants, write a diagnosis and a cure for each, and check them again in a week.

activities.record: For each plant, write: the clue, the missing need, and the cure.

flow.do: Show your child the clue chart below and read it together.
flow.say: A plant cannot tell us in words what is wrong. But they show us clues. Tall, pale and leaning means they need light. Drooping with dry soil means water. Yellow with soggy, smelly soil means too much water. Roots coming out of the hole means they need a bigger pot.
flow.kid: A plant cannot tell you in words what is wrong. But they give clues. Tall, pale, leaning: they need light. Droopy, dry soil: they need water. Yellow, soggy soil: too much water.
flow.context: This is the first step of Plant Doctor. You examine real plants for clues and work out which need is missing.

chart.title: The plant doctor's clue chart
rows: Tall, thin, pale, leaning one way
Yellow leaves, soil soggy or smelly
Air for the roots (too much water)
Water less, check the drainage hole
Roots coming out of the hole
Move them to a bigger pot
Brown, crispy leaf edges in summer sun

flow.do: Visit 5 plants. For each, check: leaves, stem, soil (press a finger in), the hole at the bottom of the pot, and which way they lean. Write a diagnosis and a cure.
flow.say: Be a plant doctor. Look, touch the soil and check the pot. Which need is missing?
flow.kid: Look at 5 plants. Check the leaves. Feel the soil. Look at the pot's hole. Which need is missing? Write it down.

ask.q: What clue told you that?
good: They were leaning towards the window.
Their leaves were droopy and the soil was dry.

flow.parent: Many home plants show more than one clue. That's normal. Ask: which clue is the strongest? Ask the owner before doing a cure.

flow.do: Choose one plant to help, with the owner's permission. Do the cure. Look again in a week.
flow.say: Let's help one plant. Then we'll see if our diagnosis was right.
flow.kid: Choose one plant to help. Do the cure. Look again in a week. Was your diagnosis right?

check.q: A money plant in a dark corridor has long gaps between their leaves and leans towards the door. Which need is missing?
check.why: Long gaps between leaves and leaning are clues of too little light. The plant is stretching towards the brightest place. Picking 'water' is common, because many sick plants need water. But a thirsty plant droops and their soil is dry.

activities.context: This is the plant doctor activity. You read the clues a real plant gives you, like drooping, yellowing or leaning, and work out which need is missing.

activities.title: The Light Map of Our Home

materials.item: a sheet of paper to draw a simple map of your home
a phone with a free light-meter app, if you have one
a white sheet of paper and a pencil, for the shadow test

activities.safety: Never look straight at the Sun, even for a moment.

schedule.what: Measure or test the light in 6 places at home. Mark them on a map. Decide where each plant should live.

activities.record: A map of your home with the brightest and darkest places marked, and where each plant should go.

flow.do: Draw a quick map of your home together: rooms, windows, the balcony and the doors.
flow.say: Let's make a map of how bright each place in our home is. Plants can't walk to the light, so we have to choose for them.
flow.kid: Draw a map of your home. Show the rooms, the windows and the balcony.
flow.context: This is the first step of the light map. You find out how bright different places in your home are, and choose where each plant should live.

flow.do: Visit 6 places: a sunny window, the middle of a room, a corridor, a bathroom, the balcony and an open window. In each place, use the light-meter app. Or hold a pencil over white paper and see how dark and sharp its shadow is.
flow.say: Our eyes are tricky. They adjust, so a room feels bright even when it is much dimmer than outside. A light meter tells the truth.
flow.kid: Go to 6 places. Measure the light with the app. Or look at a pencil's shadow. A dark, sharp shadow means bright light.

ask.q: Which place is brightest? Which is darkest?

flow.parent: Light meters measure in lux. Outdoor daylight is often tens of thousands of lux. A bright room is often a few hundred. So a room can be a hundred times dimmer than outside, even though it does not feel like it. That is why indoor plants lean to the windows. Phone apps are not exact, but they are good enough to compare places.

flow.do: Mark each place on the map: very bright, bright, dim or dark. Then decide where your home's plants should live.
flow.say: A tulsi needs lots of sun. A money plant is happy with less. Where should each of our plants go?
flow.kid: Colour each place on the map: very bright, bright, dim or dark. Draw where each plant should live.

check.q: Outside on a sunny day, and in the middle of a room: which is usually brighter, and by how much?
options: About the same, because the room feels bright
Outside, often about a hundred times brighter or more
check.why: Our eyes adjust to dim light, so a room feels bright. But a light meter shows that outside daylight is often a hundred times brighter, or more. Picking 'about the same' means trusting our eyes, which is what nearly everyone does. Plants are not fooled.

flow.think: Your eyes adjusted so well that you did not notice how dim the room was. What else might your senses be hiding from you?

activities.context: This activity maps how bright each place in your home is, using a light-meter app or shadows. Then you choose the best place for each plant.

activities.title: Bose's Growth Magnifier

materials.item: a young lobia or rajma plant, or a moong seedling at least 10 cm tall, growing in a pot or cup
a long plastic straw, about 20 cm
a pin and a small lump of clay or a cork, on top of a stick or a stack of books
a soft cotton thread about 20 cm long
a small paper clip and a strip of paper marked in centimetres

activities.safety: A grown-up handles the pin. Tie the thread loosely, so it does not cut the plant.

schedule.what: Build the straw lever and connect it to the plant in the morning. Mark the pointer every 2 hours until evening.

activities.record: Write where the pointer was every 2 hours. Work out how far it moved, and how much the plant really grew.

flow.do: Tell your child about Jagadish Chandra Bose and his crescograph.
flow.say: More than a hundred years ago, in Kolkata, Jagadish Chandra Bose built a special machine. It made a plant's growth look thousands of times bigger. Today we'll build a tiny cousin of it.
flow.kid: Long ago in Kolkata, a scientist called Bose built a machine. It made plant growth look huge. Let's build a small one.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bose's Growth Magnifier. You build a simple straw lever that makes a plant's slow growth easier to see. It is a tiny version of Jagadish Chandra Bose's crescograph.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up pushes the pin through the straw about 4 cm from one end. 2. Push the pin into the clay or cork on top of the stick, so the straw can swing like a seesaw. 3. Hang the lightest paper clip on the long end, so it tips down. 4. Tie one end of the thread loosely around the stem, just below the top leaves. 5. Tie the other end to the short end of the straw, so the thread is straight and just tight. 6. Stand the paper scale behind the long end of the straw.
flow.say: The short end is 4 centimetres from the pin. The long end is about 16 centimetres. So when the plant grows a little, the long end moves 4 times as far.
flow.kid: With a grown-up, push a pin through the straw near one end. Balance it on clay. Tie the short end to the plant's top with thread. The long end is your pointer.
flow.parent: The paper clip makes the long end heavier, so the short end keeps the thread tight. As the plant grows up, the short end can rise, and the long end drops along the scale. Use the lightest clip you have, so the thread does not pull the plant up.

flow.do: Do this in the morning. Mark where the pointer is now. Then mark it again every 2 hours until the evening.
flow.say: Let's mark the pointer every 2 hours. Is the plant growing, even while we cannot see it?
flow.kid: Mark where the pointer is. Look again every 2 hours. Mark it again. Is it moving?
flow.wait: Check every 2 hours, from morning to evening.
flow.parent: A young seedling grows about half a millimetre to one millimetre each hour on a warm day. With this lever, the pointer moves 4 millimetres for every millimetre of growth. So over a whole day it should move 2 centimetres or more. If nothing moves, check that the thread is still tight. Keep the plant away from fans and wind, which make the pointer swing.

flow.do: Work out how much the plant really grew: the pointer moved 4 times as far as the plant grew.
flow.say: The pointer moved 12 millimetres. The lever makes it look 4 times bigger. So how much did the plant really grow?
flow.kid: Measure how far the pointer moved. Divide that by 4. That is how much the plant really grew.

ask.q: If the pointer moved 12 millimetres, how much did the plant grow?

check.q: The pointer on the long end of the straw moved 8 millimetres. The long end moves 4 times as far as the plant grows. How much did the plant grow?
check.why: The lever makes growth look 4 times bigger. So the real growth is 8 divided by 4, which is 2 millimetres. Picking '32' means multiplying instead of dividing: the plant's growth is the small number, not the big one.

flow.think: Bose's machine made growth look ten thousand times bigger. He saw it speed up and slow down from minute to minute. What could make a plant grow faster for a few minutes?

activities.context: This activity builds a simple straw lever that makes a plant's growth easier to see. It is a tiny version of the crescograph, a growth-measuring machine invented by Jagadish Chandra Bose in Kolkata.

activities.title: Seedling Dance: in the dark and in the light

materials.item: a torch, or a window with sunlight
some space to move

activities.safety: Move gently and keep away from furniture edges.

schedule.what: Act out seedlings growing in the dark, in the light, in too much water and in the cold and heat.

activities.record: Draw yourself as a seedling in the dark and in the light.

flow.do: Ask your child to curl up small on the floor like a seed in the soil.
flow.say: You're a moong seed in the soil. Curl up tight. You have a little store of food inside you.
flow.kid: Curl up small like a seed. You have a little store of food inside you.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Seedling Dance. You act out how a seedling grows in the light, in the dark, and in too much water, cold and heat.

flow.do: Turn off the lights. Ask your child to grow like a seedling in the dark.
flow.say: It's dark. You can't make food. Stretch up as tall and thin as you can, fast, looking for light. Keep your hands folded shut, like small closed leaves.
flow.kid: It is dark. Stretch up tall and thin, fast. Keep your hands folded. You are looking for light!

ask.q: How does it feel to stretch and stretch?

flow.do: Shine the torch, or open the curtains. Ask your child to grow like a seedling in the light.
flow.say: Light! Now open your leaves wide, like hands catching sunshine. Stand strong and solid. You don't need to stretch so far.
flow.kid: Light! Open your hands wide like leaves. Stand strong. Turn your face to the light.
flow.think: Which seedling felt stronger: the one in the dark, or the one in the light?

flow.do: Call out other conditions and let your child act each one: soggy soil, a cold night, a heat wave, just right.
flow.say: Soggy soil! Your roots can't breathe. A cold night, 5 degrees! A heat wave, 46 degrees! Now everything is just right.
flow.kid: Act it out! Soggy soil. A cold night. A heat wave. Now everything is just right.

check.q: In the dance, a seedling in the dark stretches tall and keeps their leaves shut. Why?
options: They are using their stored food to reach light, and leaves are no use without light
check.why: Without light, leaves cannot make food. So a seedling in the dark spends their stored food on stretching up, not on opening leaves. Picking 'cold' mixes up two needs. A seedling in the cold hardly grows at all.

activities.context: This is a movement activity. Your child acts out a seedling growing in the dark and in the light, and in soggy, cold and hot conditions.

projects.title: My Bean, My Diary

materials.item: a pot about 15 cm across, with a hole in the bottom
potting soil mixed with a handful of compost
3 lobia (karamani) or rajma seeds, soaked overnight
a stick about 60 cm long for the bean to climb
a ruler, a thermometer if you have one, and a notebook

projects.safety: Wash hands after touching soil and compost. Do not eat raw rajma seeds, because they are harmful uncooked.

schedule.what: Choose the best place using your light map. Sow the beans. Name your plant. Start the diary.
Check the soil with a finger. Water if dry. Write one line in the diary.
Measure the shoot. Write the height, the weather and the temperature.
Measure. Count the leaves.
Measure. Push in the stick for climbing. Do a plant doctor check.
Measure. Draw the plant.
Measure. Did anything slow them down?
Final measuring. Draw a growth chart of all your measurements. Write what helped and what harmed your plant. Show your diary to the family.

projects.record: A diary with a page every third day: date, height, number of leaves, weather, temperature and one sentence about how the plant looks. At the end, a bar chart of the heights.

flow.do: Look at the light map from the light map activity, if you made one. Choose a bright place with some morning sun for the pot.
flow.say: Beans need lots of light, water that is just right, and warmth. Where in our home is the best place?
flow.kid: Look at your light map. Find a bright place with some morning sun. That is your bean's home.
flow.context: This is the first step of My Bean, My Diary. You grow a bean plant for three weeks, look after all their needs and keep a diary of their growth.

flow.do: 1. Fill the pot with the soil and compost. 2. Push 3 soaked beans in, about 2 cm deep and a hand-width apart. 3. Water until a little runs out of the hole. 4. Give your plant a name and write it on the pot.
flow.say: Some families talk to their plant and name them. Let's name ours. What will you call your bean?
flow.kid: Fill the pot. Push in 3 beans, 2 cm deep. Water until a little runs out of the hole. Give your plant a name!
flow.parent: Children take more care of a plant they have named. If more than one bean comes up, keep the strongest and gently pull out the others after a week, so they have space.

flow.do: Every third day: 1. Press a finger into the soil. Water only if the top is dry. 2. Measure the shoot from the soil to the tip. 3. Write the height, the number of leaves, the weather and the temperature in the diary.
flow.say: Check first, then water. Too much water drowns the roots. Then measure and write it down.
flow.kid: Every third day: feel the soil. Water only if it is dry. Measure your bean. Write it in your diary.

check.q: You press your finger into the bean's soil and it feels damp. What should you do?
options: Water them anyway, because more water is better
check.why: Damp soil already has enough water. Watering again could make it soggy, so the roots cannot get air. Picking 'water them anyway' is the most common mistake in looking after plants. Checking first is what good gardeners do.

flow.do: When the bean is about 15 cm tall, push the stick into the soil beside them, without hurting the roots.
flow.say: Many beans are climbers. Watch what the tip does with the stick in the next few days.
flow.kid: Push a stick into the soil next to your bean. Watch the tip. Will they find the stick?
flow.think: The bean has no eyes. How do they find the stick to climb?

flow.do: On Day 21: 1. Measure one last time. 2. Make a bar chart with one bar for each measuring day. 3. Write two sentences: what helped your plant grow and what slowed them down. 4. Show the diary to the family.
flow.say: Look at your chart. When did they grow fastest? Was the weather different then? What would you change next time?
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each day you measured. When did your bean grow fastest? Write what helped them and what slowed them down.

chart.title: Made-up example: my bean's height every third day
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your bean will be different.

flow.parent: If the plant dies, that is a real result too. Be a plant doctor together: which need was missing? Your child can write a short note about how it feels to lose a plant, and then try again.

challenges.title: Light for a Dark Corner
challenges.problem: A plant has to live in a dim corner, a few steps from the window. They are leaning and pale. Your job is to get more light to them without moving the pot.
constraints: Use only things from home, like white paper, cardboard, steel plates, mirrors and kitchen foil.
materials: a plant or a cup of seedlings in a dim corner
white paper, cardboard and sticky tape
kitchen foil, a steel thali or a small mirror
a light-meter app, or a pencil and white paper for the shadow test
general: Put white card or kitchen foil behind and beside the plant, so light that falls there bounces back onto the leaves.
Clean the window. A dusty window can block a lot of light.
Open the curtains wider, or tie them back.
creative: Use a steel thali or a mirror outside the window to bounce a patch of sunlight into the room. Move it every hour to follow the Sun.
Make a light funnel: line a cardboard tube with foil and point one end at the window and the other at the plant.
In some old houses in India, a small glass tile in the roof let daylight into a dark room. Could a 'skylight' of foil-lined card work for you?
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. Draw it, build it and measure the light before and after. Which idea gave the most light?

flow.do: Measure how bright the dim corner is now, with a light-meter app or the pencil-shadow test.
flow.say: First, let's measure how dark it is now, so we know if our ideas really help.
flow.kid: Measure how bright the corner is now. Use the app, or look at a pencil's shadow on white paper.
flow.context: This is the first step of Light for a Dark Corner. A plant in a dim corner needs more light, and you must bring the light to the plant without moving them.

flow.do: Before trying anything, draw or list three ideas together.
flow.say: Engineers think before they build. Let's list three ideas.
flow.kid: Think like an engineer. Draw three ideas to bring light to the corner.

flow.do: Try each idea, one at a time, and measure the light at the plant after each one.
flow.say: Try one idea at a time. Measure after each one. That's a fair test of our ideas.
flow.kid: Try your ideas one at a time. Measure the light after each one. Which works best?
flow.parent: Foil and white card usually help a little. A mirror or thali bouncing direct sunlight can help a lot, but only while the Sun is in the right place. Never point reflected sunlight at anyone's eyes.

check.q: You try foil and a clean window at the same time, and the light gets brighter. Which idea worked?
options: You can't tell, because you changed two things at once
check.why: Two things changed, so you cannot tell which one helped, or how much. Try one idea, measure, then add the next. Picking 'the foil' or 'the window' means guessing. A fair test of your ideas changes only one thing at a time.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and the creative ideas. Then invent one more.
flow.say: Here's what people usually do, and some creative ideas. Can you invent something new?
flow.kid: Look at the usual ways and the creative ideas. Now invent your own way.
flow.think: People in a crowded city also live in dim rooms. How do light and sunlight change how people feel?

challenges.title: The Holiday Waterer
challenges.problem: Your family is going away for 7 days. Your plant must have water that is just right the whole time: not dry, and not soaked. Design a way to water them while you are away.
constraints: Nobody can visit the plant for 7 days.
The soil must not get soggy, because roots need air.
materials: a potted plant, or a cup of seedlings
plastic bottles, cotton string or a strip of old cloth, a small clay pot or matka if you have one
a nail for a grown-up to make small holes
general: Fill a plastic bottle with water, make a tiny hole in the cap, and push it upside down into the soil. It drips slowly.

Put a jug of water beside the pot, standing a little higher than the soil. Bury one end of a cotton string in the soil and put the other end in the water. The string soaks up water and carries it to the soil, a little at a time.
Move the plant to a shadier, cooler place, so they lose less water while you are away.
creative: Bury a small unglazed clay pot full of water in a big pot of soil, with its mouth just above the soil. Water seeps slowly through the clay. Farmers in India and many other places have watered plants with buried clay pots for a very long time.

Put the plant in a clear plastic bag, loosely, like a tiny greenhouse. Water that evaporates from the leaves collects on the bag and drips back into the soil. Do not seal it tight, and keep it out of direct sun.
Group all your plants together on a tray of damp pebbles. They keep each other's air moist.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. Test it for 3 days before your trip and check the soil each day. Is it dry, damp or soggy?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask: what does just-right water mean for this plant?
flow.say: We need to give the plant water slowly, a little every day. Too much at once, and the roots drown.
flow.kid: Your plant needs water for 7 days while you are away. Not too little. Not too much. How could you do it?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Holiday Waterer. It is an engineering challenge: keep a plant's water just right for 7 days with nobody at home.

flow.do: Draw three ideas together. Then build the one your child likes best.
flow.say: Let's draw three ideas, then build the best one.
flow.kid: Draw three ideas. Then build the best one. Ask a grown-up for help with holes.

flow.do: Test the waterer on the plant for 3 days. Check the soil each day with a finger and write: dry, damp or soggy.
flow.say: A good engineer tests before the trip. Let's check the soil every day.
flow.kid: Test your waterer for 3 days. Feel the soil each day. Dry, damp or soggy? Write it down.
flow.wait: Check the soil once a day for 3 days.

flow.do: Look at the results. Fix the design if the soil was dry or soggy, and test it again.
flow.say: Was the soil just right every day? If not, what will you change?
flow.kid: Was the soil just right? If it was dry, give more water. If it was soggy, give less. Fix it and test again.

check.q: Your bottle waterer made the soil soggy by the second day. What should you change?
options: Make the hole in the cap bigger
Make the hole smaller, so the water comes out more slowly
check.why: Soggy soil means water is coming in faster than the plant uses it. A smaller hole slows the drip. A bigger hole lets the water out even faster. A bigger bottle holds more water, but it does not slow the drip. Remember, roots need air too.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative solutions. Then invent one more, and choose the one to use on your real trip.
flow.say: Here's what people usually do, and some clever old ideas. Which will we use for the real trip?
flow.kid: Look at the usual ways and the creative ideas. Can you invent a better one?
flow.think: The buried clay pot idea is very old. Why do you think people kept using it for so long?

quiz.p: Which list shows what a plant needs to grow well?
opts: Only soil and water
Darkness, water and soil
Light, water, air, warmth and minerals
quiz.why: Plants need light, water, air, warmth and minerals. Picking 'only soil and water' leaves out light, which plants use to make food, and air for their roots and leaves.

opts: You change everything at once
You change only one thing and keep everything else the same
You test only one plant
quiz.why: Changing only one thing tells you what caused the result. Picking 'test only one plant' misses that one plant can be a fluke.

quiz.p: In the light test, you forget to water the dark cups. What is wrong with the test?
opts: Two things changed, light and water, so you can't tell which caused the result
Nothing
The cups were too small
quiz.why: A fair test changes only one thing. Picking 'nothing' means noticing the planned change but not the accidental one.
quiz.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.

quiz.p: A girl measures her moong seedlings at 7 in the morning one day, and at 9 at night the next day. Why is it better to measure at the same time every day?
opts: Plants grow only in the morning
Rulers are easier to read in the morning
So the gap between measurements is always one whole day, and the numbers can be compared fairly
quiz.why: Seedlings grow all day and all night. If the gaps are different lengths, a bigger number may only mean a longer gap. Picking 'plants grow only in the morning' is not right: Bose's crescograph showed plants growing at night too.

quiz.p: A seedling is 6 centimetres and 5 millimetres tall. How many millimetres is that?
opts: 11 millimetres
65 millimetres
6.5 millimetres
quiz.why: Each centimetre is 10 millimetres. So 6 centimetres is 60 millimetres, and 5 more makes 65. Picking 11 means adding 6 and 5 without changing the units.

quiz.p: Look at the chart. Which cup's seedlings grew taller?
opts: DARK
LIGHT
They were the same
quiz.why: The DARK bar is taller: 14 cm against 8 cm. But remember, the dark ones were pale and weak. Picking LIGHT means answering 'which was healthier' instead of 'which was taller'.
quiz.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.

chart.title: The light test: middle height on Day 7 (made-up results)

quiz.p: Which sentence is a good conclusion for the water test?
opts: Plants are nice.
I watered the plants.
We found that the JUST RIGHT seedlings grew tallest, at 13 cm. This shows moong needs some water, but not too much.
quiz.why: A good conclusion says what was found, uses a number as proof, and says what it shows. Picking 'I watered the plants' describes what you did, not what you found.
quiz.context: This question is about the water test. Three cups of moong get no water. Three get 1 tablespoon of water every morning. Three stand in a dish of water all the time.

quiz.p: It is the monsoon in Kochi, with weeks of thick grey cloud. Seedlings on a windowsill get water and warmth, but they grow slowly and lean towards the glass. Which need is in short supply?
opts: Water
Light
Minerals
quiz.why: Thick cloud blocks much of the sunlight, so the seedlings lean towards the brightest place. Picking 'water' misses that the monsoon gives plenty of water. It is the light that is short.

quiz.p: A tulsi has lived in the same small pot of soil for three years. The tulsi gets good light and the right amount of water. But the new leaves are small and pale. What might help?
opts: Fresh soil or a little compost, because the old soil's minerals are used up
Moving the tulsi to a dark corner
Watering the tulsi twice as much
quiz.why: Each year the roots take minerals out of the soil, and in a small pot nothing puts them back. Pale, small new leaves are a clue that minerals are short. Picking 'twice as much water' would soak the soil and take away the roots' air.

quiz.p: Is more water always better for a plant?
opts: Yes
No. Roots need air too, and soaked soil drowns them
quiz.why: Each need must be just right. Picking 'yes' is one of the most common mistakes in caring for plants.

quiz.p: Which is true about warmth and plants?
opts: The hotter, the faster they grow, with no limit
Plants grow fastest in the fridge
Warmth speeds up growth, but too much heat harms plants
quiz.why: Each plant has a just-right range. Picking 'no limit' misses that great heat harms the plant's helper molecules.

quiz.p: Why is wheat sown in the cool winter in Punjab?
opts: Wheat needs a flooded field
Wheat grows best in cool weather
Wheat cannot grow in sunlight
quiz.why: Each crop has their own just right. Wheat likes it cool. Picking 'a flooded field' describes rice, not wheat.

quiz.p: How does a seedling in the dark sense that it is dark?
opts: With special light-sensing molecules, such as phytochrome
With tiny eyes on their leaves
They cannot sense light
quiz.why: Plants have photoreceptor molecules that change in light. Picking 'eyes' gives plants an animal body part they don't have.

quiz.p: Astronauts grow lettuce on the International Space Station, inside a closed box. Which need do the box's pink-purple lamps give the plants?
opts: Water
Minerals
Light
quiz.why: The lamps give light, mostly red and blue, the colours leaves use most. Water and minerals come from a pillow of soil-like material. Picking 'water' mixes up what a lamp gives with what a watering can gives.

quiz.p: Jagadish Chandra Bose built the crescograph, a machine that made a plant's growth look thousands of times bigger. What did it show?
opts: That plants never grow at night
That a plant's growth speeds up and slows down from minute to minute
That plants grow only when someone is watching
quiz.why: Bose saw a plant's growth change within minutes, for example when they were touched or warmed. Plants respond to what is around them all the time. Picking 'never at night' is wrong: plants grow at night too.

applications: Farmers sow each crop in the season whose warmth and rain suit it. Rabi wheat is sown in winter, and kharif rice in the monsoon.
Greenhouses and polyhouses keep plants warm and protected, so farmers can grow vegetables out of season.
Drip irrigation gives each plant just the right water, drop by drop, and saves a lot of water. Many Indian farms use it.
Plant nurseries put sun-loving plants in full sun and shade-loving plants under green shade nets.
Hydroponic farms on city rooftops grow lettuce, spinach and herbs in mineral water with no soil.
Grow lights in vertical farms and space gardens often use red and blue lamps, the colours plants use most.
Seed banks keep seeds cold and dry so they stay alive for many years.
Fair tests are used by scientists who breed new crops, to find out which kind grows best in heat or drought.
Weather forecasts help farmers decide when to sow and when to water.
Space agencies are testing how to grow food for long journeys to the Moon and Mars.
Gardeners use pots with drainage holes and add sand to heavy soil, so roots get air.
Botanic gardens keep plants from deserts, rainforests and mountains alive by copying the light, water and warmth of their homes.

open_questions.q: Exactly how does a plant feel warmth?
open_questions.why_open: In 2016 scientists found that a light-sensing molecule, phytochrome B, also senses warmth. Since then they have found other warmth-sensing molecules. How they all work together is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Why does a plant's growth speed up and slow down from minute to minute?
open_questions.why_open: Jagadish Chandra Bose saw this with his crescograph over a hundred years ago. Scientists now know many signals are involved, from light and warmth to water and the plant's own daily clock. But the whole picture is still not clear.

open_questions.q: How will India's crops cope as summers get hotter?
open_questions.why_open: In 2022, an early heat wave in March shrank India's wheat harvest. Scientists are breeding crops that cope better with heat, but nobody knows yet how well they will keep up.

open_questions.q: Could we grow food in the soil of the Moon or Mars?
open_questions.why_open: In 2022, small plants grew in real Moon soil, but slowly, and they showed signs of stress. Mars soil contains harmful salts. Scientists are still testing ways to make these soils safe for plants.

open_questions.q: Do plants respond to sound in useful ways?
open_questions.why_open: Some experiments show plants react to the vibrations of chewing insects, or of running water. Others find nothing. It is hard to test fairly, and scientists still argue.

open_questions.q: How does a seedling decide how to share their stored food between roots, stem and leaves?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that light, water and minerals all change the decision, through plant hormones. How a plant without a brain balances all of these is still being studied.

maths.problem: In the light test, a seedling was 3 cm tall on Day 3 and 8 cm tall on Day 7. How much did they grow between Day 3 and Day 7?
maths.explain: The seedling was 8 cm on Day 7 and 3 cm on Day 3. 8 take away 3 is 5. So they grew 5 cm. You can check: 3 + 5 = 8.
maths.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.
maths.why_maths: A ruler tells you how tall a plant is. Taking away yesterday's height from today's tells you how much they grew, which is what we really want to know.

maths.problem: Look at the ruler in the picture. The top of a seedling is at the arrow, halfway between 6 and 7. Each big number is a centimetre. How tall is the seedling, in centimetres and in millimetres?
maths.answer: 6 and a half centimetres, which is 65 millimetres.
maths.explain: The arrow is past the 6, halfway to the 7. Halfway is 5 tiny millimetre marks. So the seedling is 6 centimetres and 5 millimetres. Each centimetre is 10 millimetres, so 6 centimetres is 60 millimetres. 60 + 5 = 65 millimetres.
maths.context: In this unit you measure seedlings with a ruler every day. The big numbers on a ruler are centimetres. The tiny marks between them are millimetres. Ten millimetres make one centimetre.

chart.title: A ruler, measuring in centimetres
chart.label: Each tiny mark is 1 millimetre. Halfway between two numbers is 5 millimetres.

maths.why_maths: Seedlings grow only a few millimetres a day. Reading the tiny marks on a ruler lets you see growth that whole centimetres would miss.

maths.problem: In the warmth test, you put a thermometer in each place. Look at the thermometer in the picture. What temperature does it show?
maths.explain: The red line stops at the mark 2 above the 25. Each mark is 1 degree. So the temperature is 25 + 2 = 27 degrees Celsius. That is the temperature of the room cupboard.
maths.context: This question is about the warmth test. Moong sprouts are kept in the dark in a fridge, a room cupboard and a warm spot, and measured each day.

chart.title: A room thermometer, in degrees Celsius (°C)
chart.label: Each small mark is 1 degree.

maths.why_maths: To know if warmth changes growth, you must know how warm each place really was. A thermometer only helps if you can read it.

maths.problem: Look at the bar chart from the water test. How much taller was the JUST RIGHT group than the SOAKED group?
maths.explain: The JUST RIGHT bar reaches 13 cm and the SOAKED bar reaches 8 cm. 13 take away 8 is 5. So the JUST RIGHT seedlings were 5 cm taller.
maths.context: This question is about the water test. Three cups of moong get no water. Three get 1 tablespoon of water every morning. Three stand in a dish of water all the time.

chart.title: The water test: middle height on Day 14 (made-up results)

maths.why_maths: After a test you have a list of numbers. A bar chart shows the best group at a glance, and reading two bars tells you how big the difference is.

maths.problem: In the light test, the three DARK cups measured 13 cm, 15 cm and 14 cm. What is the middle value?
maths.explain: Put the numbers in order: 13, 14, 15. The one in the middle is 14. So the middle value is 14 cm.
maths.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.
maths.why_maths: Three cups never give exactly the same number. The middle value gives one fair number for the group, and stops one odd cup from fooling us.

maths.problem: In the warmth test, the 5 longest sprouts in the warm bowl added up to 6 cm on Day 1. On Day 4 they added up to 30 cm. How much did they grow? How much is that for each sprout, on average?
maths.answer: They grew 24 cm altogether. That is a little under 5 cm for each sprout.
maths.explain: 30 take away 6 is 24. So the 5 sprouts grew 24 cm altogether. 24 shared between 5 sprouts is 4 each, with 4 cm left over. Sharing those 4 cm as well gives each sprout almost 1 cm more. So each sprout grew a little under 5 cm.
maths.context: This question is about the warmth test. Moong sprouts are kept in the dark in a fridge, a room cupboard and a warm spot, and measured each day.
maths.why_maths: Adding up 5 sprouts gives one number for each bowl. Sharing it back out tells you how much a single sprout grew.

roots.context: We have been finding out what a plant needs, with fair tests of light, water and warmth. Now we ask what a plant's needs tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: The same moong seeds grew short and green in the light, and tall and pale in the dark. The seeds came from one packet and got the same water. The light they sensed decided how they grew. So one kind of seed can grow into very different plants, depending on what they find where they grow.
deep_truth.habit: We think a living thing's shape comes from inside them, already set in the seed. But a seed brings only part of the plan. The light, water and warmth they meet finish the rest.
deep_truth.evidence: In the light test, moong in the light grew short and green, with open leaves. The same seeds under the box grew tall, pale and thin, with leaves still closed. Back in the light, the pale ones began to turn green within a day.

three.who_am_i: Your body also changes with where and how you live. Skin gets darker in strong sun, and muscles grow stronger with use.
three.what_is_life: A living thing keeps sensing the world and changing to fit it. Too little or too much of a need changes how they grow.
three.what_is_this_world: The light that shapes a seedling on your windowsill left the Sun about eight minutes earlier. So a star 150 million kilometres away helps shape a plant in your home.

roots.thread: A moong seed holds the start of a plant: a tiny root, a tiny shoot and a store of food. But the plant they become depends on what they meet. Light, water, warmth and air all change their shape as they grow. A living thing and their world keep making each other. A seedling senses their place from their first day, and grows to fit it.

teachings.teaching: From the Self came space. From space came air. From air came fire, and from fire came water. From water came earth, from earth came plants, and from plants came food.
teachings.link: The Upanishad puts plants after air, fire, water and earth, as if they are made from all of them. Our tests give the same list from science: a plant needs air, warmth and light, water, and minerals from the earth.

teachings.source: Samyutta Nikaya 56.11, the Buddha's first teaching
teachings.teaching: The Buddha said that two extremes, too much comfort and too much hardship, do not lead anywhere good. He taught a middle way between them.
teachings.link: The Buddha was talking about how people live, not about plants. But our water test has the same shape: no water and too much water both harm a moong seedling, and they grow best in between.

science.text: The same seeds can grow into very different shapes in different light, water and warmth. Biologists call this power to change shape to fit the surroundings plasticity.
Sunlight takes about eight minutes to travel from the Sun to a leaf.

other_view.view: Jain thinkers teach that each plant has their own soul, called a jiva, separate from every other soul. On this view, a seedling turns to the light because they are a living being in their own right, not because they and the world are one.

practice.title: Sun and shade

how_we_found_out.context: Does a plant need anything from the soil, or only water? This card tells the true story of how people found out.
how_we_found_out.story: In the 1600s, Jan Baptist van Helmont, a scientist in what is now Belgium, grew a willow tree in a pot of soil for five years. He gave the tree only rainwater. The tree gained about 74 kilograms, but the soil lost only about 57 grams. So he decided that a plant is made from water alone. In 1699, John Woodward, an English doctor, tested this idea. If plants are made only of water, he thought, then the purest water should grow them best. He put sprigs of spearmint in glass jars of different water: rainwater, water from the river Thames, and water with some garden soil stirred in. For several weeks he weighed the plants and the water they used. The mint in the muddiest water grew the most. The mint in clean rainwater grew the least. So plants take something from the soil, carried in the water. Today we call these things minerals. Woodward also found that most of the water a plant takes in goes out through their leaves into the air.
how_we_found_out.who: Jan Baptist van Helmont, in what is now Belgium (1600s); John Woodward, an English doctor (1699)
how_we_found_out.when: Van Helmont's willow in the early 1600s, written up in 1648; Woodward's mint test in 1699
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a plant is made from water alone. Woodward's mint grew better in muddy water than in pure rainwater, so something from the soil helps them grow. Woodward then went too far the other way and thought plants are made mostly of soil. Later scientists found that most of a plant's weight comes from the air, as the unit Food from light explains.
how_we_found_out.art: A row of glass jars on a windowsill, each holding a sprig of mint: clear rainwater, river water and cloudy muddy water, with the mint in the muddy jar the biggest.
